                output_var="DynamicOutput" />

        <script id="LogDynamicOutput" language="powershell">
            <![CDATA[
            Write-Host "Result of dynamic execution: {{DynamicOutput}}"
            ]]>
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 6. Error Handling & Retry Policies
docs.text:
When a script fails (e.g. non-zero exit code, unhandled Go panic, or timeout expiration), the <script> node responds according to on_error:

<!-- Stop on failure (Default) -->
<script id="CriticalStep" language="go" on_error="stop">
    ...
</script>

<!-- Continue execution on failure -->
<script id="OptionalStep" language="bash" on_error="continue">
    ...
</script>

<!-- Automatic retry with exponential or fixed backoff -->
<script id="FlakyNetworkCall"
        language="go"
        on_error="retry"
        retry_count="3"
        retry_interval="5s"
        timeout="15s">
    ...
</script>

docs.title: 7. Summary & Quick Reference
docs.text: Goal Recommended Approach Max portability (Windows, Linux, macOS) Use <script language="go"> with "host/vars". Requires zero host dependencies. Pass data between steps Use output_var="VarName" to capture stdout, or vars.SetString("VarName", val) in Go. Access pipeline variables in script Use {{VarName}} anywhere in the body, or vars.GetString("VarName") in Go. Prevent XML parsing errors Always enclose script bodies inside <![CDATA[ ... ]]>. Prevent runaway executions Set timeout="30s" or timeout="5m". Enforce database prerequisites Use language="go" with "host/db" to probe connections before running large bulk ETL jobs.

docs.title: SQL Query & Command Node (<sql>) Guide 🚀
docs.text: The <sql> node executes native SQL scripts, queries, and multi-statement database commands directly on any registered database connection. It is engineered for relational database workloads ranging from simple single-statement lookups to massive multi-million-row in-database transformations and data warehouse consolidations.

docs.title: 📋 Attribute Specifications
docs.text: Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier across the pipeline. db / database Yes — Name of the database configured in the <databases> section. output_var / into / var No — Pipeline variable name to capture returned query result sets (as JSON arrays) or affected row counts. timeout No — Execution deadline duration (e.g. 30s, 5m, 45m). condition / cond No — Condition expression required to execute this step. on_error No stop Failure handling strategy: stop, continue, or retry. retry_count No 0 Number of retries on transient connection or query errors. retry_interval No 1s Duration between retries (e.g. 2s, 500ms). description No — Human-readable explanation of this SQL operation.

docs.title: 🧠 Intelligent Query vs. DML Classification (isDMLQuery)
docs.text:
Flow features a built-in token-aware SQL analyzer that automatically distinguishes between data retrieval (SELECT, SHOW, WITH) and data mutation (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, CREATE, DROP):

  1. Comments & CDATA Stripping: Leading/trailing single-line comments (-- ...), multi-line comments (/* ... */), and XML <![CDATA[ ... ]]> tags are cleanly stripped before token evaluation.
  2. Column Name Collision Safety: Queries selecting columns named deleted_at, is_deleted, insert_ts, or update_count are correctly classified as queries and are not misclassified as DML mutations.
  3. Row-Returning Mutations: Statements utilizing clauses like RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle) or OUTPUT (SQL Server) are executed as queries so returned rows are preserved in output_var.
  4. Summary Selects & Rowcounts: Complex multi-statement batches that conclude with a scalar summary (such as SELECT @@ROWCOUNT; or SELECT count(*);) return that scalar value directly into output_var.

docs.title: 🔒 Atomic Transactions with <group transaction="true">
docs.text:
To coordinate multiple <sql> steps inside an atomic database transaction with automatic commit and rollback:

<group id="financial_batch" transaction="true" db="main_db" timeout="2m">
    <sql id="debit_account" db="main_db">
        UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 250 WHERE id = 101;
    </sql>
    <sql id="credit_account" db="main_db">
        UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 250 WHERE id = 202;
    </sql>
</group>
  • Dialect-Aware Savepoints: Nested groups on the same database automatically use savepoints (SAVE TRANSACTION on MSSQL, ANSI SAVEPOINT on PostgreSQL/SQLite/MySQL).
  • Deferred Rollback: If any child step errors, the entire transaction (or nested savepoint) is rolled back before propagation.

docs.title: Example 1: Schema Initialization & Table Setup (DDL)
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="reporting_db" driver="sqlite" connection_string="./reporting.db" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <sql id="init_schema" db="reporting_db" description="Initialize reporting tables">
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS customer_daily_summary (
                customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                total_spend REAL NOT NULL,
                last_order_date TEXT NOT NULL,
                status TEXT DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
            );
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_cust_status ON customer_daily_summary(status);
        </sql>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Data Extraction into Pipeline Variable
docs.text:
Extracting rows into a pipeline variable formats the result as a structured JSON array suitable for downstream loops, assertions, or templates:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="oltp_pg" driver="postgres" connection_string="postgresql://app:secret@localhost:5432/appdb" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <sql id="get_top_spenders" 
             db="oltp_pg" 
             output_var="VIP_CUSTOMERS"
             timeout="30s">
            SELECT 
                customer_id, 
                full_name, 
                lifetime_value, 
                country_code
            FROM customers
            WHERE lifetime_value >= 10000.00
            ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC
            LIMIT 50;
        </sql>

        <!-- Assert that high spenders were retrieved -->
        <assert id="check_vip_count" 
                var="VIP_CUSTOMERS" 
                condition="count(VIP_CUSTOMERS) > 0" 
                message="Expected at least one VIP customer." />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: Multi-Stage Enterprise ETL Batch Returning SELECT @@ROWCOUNT
docs.text:
This production pattern runs in-database transformations across millions of rows in SQL Server without transferring heavy intermediate datasets across the network:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="dw_sqlserver" 
                  driver="sqlserver" 
                  connection_string="sqlserver://etl:P@ssword1@dw.internal:1433?database=EnterpriseDW"
                  workload="bulk" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <sql id="nightly_consolidation" 
             db="dw_sqlserver" 
             timeout="45m"
             output_var="ROWS_PROCESSED">
            <![CDATA[
            SET NOCOUNT ON;
            SET XACT_ABORT ON;

            BEGIN TRANSACTION;

            -- 1. Deduplicate raw incoming events into staging temp table
            IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#StagedEvents') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #StagedEvents;

            CREATE TABLE #StagedEvents (
                EventKey BIGINT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
                AccountID INT NOT NULL,
                Amount DECIMAL(18,4) NOT NULL,
                EventTimestamp DATETIME2(3) NOT NULL
            );

            INSERT INTO #StagedEvents WITH (TABLOCK)
            SELECT EventKey, AccountID, Amount, EventTimestamp
            FROM (
                SELECT EventKey, AccountID, Amount, EventTimestamp,
                       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY EventKey ORDER BY IngestTimestamp DESC) AS rn
                FROM Ingest.RawEvents
                WHERE ProcessingStatus = 'PENDING'
            ) t WHERE t.rn = 1;

            -- 2. Upsert into production Fact table
            MERGE INTO Fact.AccountEvents WITH (TABLOCK) AS tgt
            USING #StagedEvents AS src
            ON (tgt.EventKey = src.EventKey)
            WHEN MATCHED THEN
                UPDATE SET tgt.Amount = src.Amount, tgt.LastModifiedUTC = GETUTCDATE()
            WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
                INSERT (EventKey, AccountID, Amount, EventTimestamp, CreatedUTC)
                VALUES (src.EventKey, src.AccountID, src.Amount, src.EventTimestamp, GETUTCDATE());

            -- 3. Mark processed in raw ledger
            UPDATE raw
            SET raw.ProcessingStatus = 'PROCESSED'
            FROM Ingest.RawEvents raw
            INNER JOIN #StagedEvents stg ON raw.EventKey = stg.EventKey;

            DROP TABLE #StagedEvents;

            COMMIT TRANSACTION;

            -- 4. Return strictly scalar rowcount to Flow output variable
            SELECT @@ROWCOUNT AS affected_rows;
            ]]>
        </sql>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 4: PostgreSQL RETURNING Clause Capturing Inserted Rows
docs.text:
<sql id="insert_and_capture_ids" db="oltp_pg" output_var="INSERTED_RECORDS">
    INSERT INTO order_audit (order_id, action, performed_by)
    VALUES 
        (1001, 'APPROVED', 'system'),
        (1002, 'APPROVED', 'system')
    RETURNING id, order_id, created_at;
</sql>

docs.title: 🛠️ Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep Heavy Data in the Engine: When transforming existing database records, use <sql> with in-database SQL (MERGE, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, UPDATE ... JOIN) rather than pulling millions of records into Go memory.
  2. End Multi-Statement Batches with a Scalar Query: When executing DDL/DML batches where you need telemetry metrics, conclude with SELECT @@ROWCOUNT; or SELECT count(*);.
  3. Use CDATA for Complex Queries: Enclose SQL containing comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=) or & characters within <![CDATA[ ... ]]> to prevent XML parsing syntax errors.
  4. Tune Timeouts: Always set explicit timeout="5m" or timeout="30m" for long-running batches to prevent indefinite pipeline hangs on locked resources.

docs.title: SQL and SQL Bulk Operations Guide 🚀
docs.text: The Flow execution engine provides first-class support for relational database workloads ranging from simple single-statement lookups to massive multi-million-row streaming replications and multi-stage enterprise data warehouse transforms.

docs.title: 🎯 Workload Recommendation Matrix: What Node & Options Should You Use?
docs.text:
Choosing the right node and tuning configuration is critical for achieving optimal throughput, minimizing connection contention, and avoiding memory or transaction bottlenecks.

Workload Scenario Recommended Node Key Options & Attributes Rationale & Performance Impact Schema Initialization (DDL) & Basic Queries <sql> db="db_name"output_var="MY_VAR" Direct execution. Statements returning rows (SELECT, SHOW, WITH) format outputs into output_var. Complex In-Database ETL / Multi-Stage Transformations <sql> db="db_name"output_var="ROW_COUNT" Ideal for heavy in-database processing (CTEs, MERGE, temp tables, indexing). Keeps data inside the database engine; ends with SELECT @@ROWCOUNT or summary scalar. Cross-Database Table Replication (e.g. Postgres → SQL Server) <sql_bulk> db="src_db"target_db="dst_db"target_table="fact_table"batch_size="10000" Streams rows across disparate engines with constant $O(1)$ memory. Eliminates intermediate CSV/JSON files and memory bloat. High-Throughput SQL Server Ingestion <sql_bulk> tablock="true"check_constraints="false"batch_size="25000" Activates SQL Server minimal logging (TABLOCK) and disables constraint checking during bulk insertion for maximum MB/sec throughput. Preserving Identity & Explicit NULLs during Bulk Copies <sql_bulk> keep_nulls="true"fire_triggers="false" Prevents default column constraints from replacing explicit NULL values during bulk ingestion. Multi-Step Atomic Transactions with Rollback <group> + <sql> transaction="true"db="db_name"timeout="60s" Wraps multiple child <sql> steps in a single atomic transaction. Automatically leverages dialect-aware savepoints (SAVE TRANSACTION for MSSQL, ANSI SAVEPOINT for PostgreSQL/SQLite/MySQL) for nested groups on the same database. Row-by-Row Dynamic Operations (e.g. Webhook / API per record) <foreach> + <sql> db="db_name"buffer="false" (default) Streams rows one-by-one into child tasks with constant memory, safely handling 60M+ rows. Use buffer="true" only for small control sets (<100k rows) to release DB locks early.

docs.title: Decision Flowchart
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Start["Incoming Database Task"] --> Q1{"Are you moving data across tables or different databases?"}

    Q1 -- "Yes (Replication / Ingestion)" --> Q2{"Are you transforming rows in Go or calling external APIs per row?"}
    Q2 -- "No (Direct Copy)" --> Bulk["Use <sql_bulk><br>• Set batch_size=10000-50000<br>• Enable tablock for MSSQL<br>• Zero RAM footprint"]
    Q2 -- "Yes (Row-by-Row APIs/Scripts)" --> ForEach["Use <foreach><br>• Default streaming mode: O(1) RAM<br>• Sub-millisecond cursor fetch"]

    Q1 -- "No (In-Database Processing)" --> Q3{"Do multiple steps require atomic commit / rollback?"}
    Q3 -- "Yes" --> GroupTx["Wrap in <group transaction='true' db='...'><br>• Automatic SAVEPOINT nesting<br>• Safe deferred rollbacks"]
    Q3 -- "No" --> SqlNode["Use standard <sql><br>• Supports DDL, DML, CTEs, MERGE<br>• Intelligent query vs DML detection<br>• Captures SELECT @@ROWCOUNT"]

docs.title: 1. The <sql> Node
docs.text: The <sql> node executes native SQL scripts directly on a registered database handle.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier across the pipeline. db / database Yes — Name of the database configured in <databases>. output_var / var No — Name of pipeline variable to capture the returned query result set or affected row count. timeout No — Execution deadline duration (e.g., 30s, 5m).

docs.title: Intelligent Query vs. DML Classification (isDMLQuery)
docs.text: Flow features a built-in token-aware SQL analyzer: - Comments & CDATA Stripping: Comments (-- ..., /* ... */) and XML CDATA sections are cleanly stripped prior to token inspection. - Column Name Safety: Queries selecting columns named deleted_at, is_deleted, insert_ts, or update_count are recognized as standard queries and are not misclassified as DML statements. - Row-Returning Mutations: Statements utilizing clauses like RETURNING (Postgres, SQLite, Oracle) or OUTPUT (SQL Server) are executed as queries so returned rows are preserved in output_var. - Summary Selects: Complex multi-statement DML batches that conclude with a scalar summary (such as SELECT @@ROWCOUNT;) return that scalar result directly to output_var.

docs.title: 2. The <sql_bulk> Node
docs.text: The <sql_bulk> node is an optimized streaming pipeline primitive that pipes rows from a source SQL query directly into a destination table.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier. db / database Yes — Source database connection handle. target_db No Source db Destination database connection handle. target_table Yes — Destination table name receiving bulk inserts. batch_size No 10000 Number of rows committed per network chunk. tablock No true (SQL Server) Acquires table-level lock for minimal transaction logging. check_constraints No false (SQL Server) Validates foreign keys/check constraints during bulk load. fire_triggers No false (SQL Server) Fires insert triggers on the target table during bulk load. keep_nulls No false (SQL Server) Preserves incoming NULL values instead of replacing with column defaults. output_var No — Stores total number of rows streamed to destination.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple SQL Query and Bulk Copy
docs.text:
A clean, minimal example demonstrating table setup, standard <sql> querying into a pipeline variable, and cross-database <sql_bulk> replication.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="oltp_db" driver="postgres" connection_string="postgresql://app:secret@localhost:5432/orders_app" />
        <database name="reporting_db" driver="sqlite" connection_string="./reporting.db" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- 1. Simple SQL: Initialize target reporting table -->
        <sql id="init_reporting_schema" db="reporting_db">
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS customer_daily_spend (
                customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                total_amount REAL,
                order_date TEXT
            );
        </sql>

        <!-- 2. Simple SQL Bulk: Stream aggregated results from Postgres to SQLite -->
        <sql_bulk id="sync_daily_spend"
                  db="oltp_db"
                  target_db="reporting_db"
                  target_table="customer_daily_spend"
                  batch_size="5000"
                  output_var="RECORDS_SYNCED">
            SELECT 
                customer_id, 
                SUM(amount) AS total_amount, 
                CAST(order_date AS TEXT) AS order_date
            FROM orders
            WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
            GROUP BY customer_id, order_date;
        </sql_bulk>

        <!-- 3. Simple SQL: Query the row count from the destination table -->
        <sql id="verify_sync" db="reporting_db" output_var="VERIFY_COUNT">
            SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_synced_customers FROM customer_daily_spend;
        </sql>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Complex Enterprise SQL Transform on Millions of Rows Returning SELECT @@ROWCOUNT
docs.text:
This production-grade script executes a high-volume data warehouse consolidation across tens of millions of records on Microsoft SQL Server. It performs: 1. Temporary table creation with clustered columnstore and primary key hints. 2. Deduplication using window functions (ROW_NUMBER()). 3. High-volume MERGE into a target fact table (handling inserts and updates in a single pass). 4. Cascading updates to audit ledger status records. 5. Index reorganization on modified partitions. 6. Returns exclusively SELECT @@ROWCOUNT so the pipeline captures the total affected rows without transmitting massive intermediate datasets over the wire.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="dw_sqlserver" 
                  driver="sqlserver" 
                  connection_string="sqlserver://etl_user:P@ssw0rd123@sql-dw.corp.internal:1433?database=EnterpriseDW&encrypt=true"
                  max_open_conns="50"
                  max_idle_conns="10"
                  workload="bulk" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Complex Enterprise Batch: Executes multi-stage transforms on millions of rows, returning only @@ROWCOUNT -->
        <sql id="execute_nightly_warehouse_consolidation" 
             db="dw_sqlserver" 
             timeout="45m"
             output_var="TOTAL_ROWS_AFFECTED">
            <![CDATA[
            SET NOCOUNT ON;
            SET XACT_ABORT ON;

            BEGIN TRANSACTION;

            -- 1. Create optimized staging structure in tempdb
            IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#StagedEvents') IS NOT NULL 
                DROP TABLE #StagedEvents;

            CREATE TABLE #StagedEvents (
                EventKey BIGINT NOT NULL,
                AccountID INT NOT NULL,
                EventCode VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
                PayloadAmount DECIMAL(18,4) NOT NULL,
                EventTimestamp DATETIME2(3) NOT NULL,
                RowHash VARBINARY(32) NOT NULL,
                DedupRank INT NOT NULL,
                INDEX IX_StagedEvents_Key CLUSTERED (EventKey, AccountID)
            );

            -- 2. Populate staging and filter duplicates across 15M+ raw ingest records
            INSERT INTO #StagedEvents WITH (TABLOCK)
            SELECT 
                r.EventKey,
                r.AccountID,
                r.EventCode,
                r.PayloadAmount,
                r.EventTimestamp,
                HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', CONCAT(r.EventKey, '|', r.AccountID, '|', r.PayloadAmount, '|', r.EventTimestamp)) AS RowHash,
                ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                    PARTITION BY r.EventKey, r.AccountID 
                    ORDER BY r.IngestTimestamp DESC, r.SequenceID DESC
                ) AS DedupRank
            FROM RawIngest.IncomingEvents r WITH (NOLOCK)
            WHERE r.IngestDate >= CAST(DATEADD(DAY, -1, GETUTCDATE()) AS DATE)
              AND r.ProcessingStatus = 'PENDING';

            -- 3. Perform High-Volume MERGE into Production Fact Table
            MERGE INTO Fact.AccountTransactions WITH (TABLOCK) AS tgt
            USING (
                SELECT 
                    EventKey,
                    AccountID,
                    EventCode,
                    PayloadAmount,
                    EventTimestamp,
                    RowHash
                FROM #StagedEvents
                WHERE DedupRank = 1
            ) AS src
            ON (tgt.EventKey = src.EventKey AND tgt.AccountID = src.AccountID)

            -- Update existing records if payload or hash has evolved
            WHEN MATCHED AND tgt.RowHash <> src.RowHash THEN
                UPDATE SET 
                    tgt.EventCode = src.EventCode,
                    tgt.PayloadAmount = src.PayloadAmount,
                    tgt.EventTimestamp = src.EventTimestamp,
                    tgt.RowHash = src.RowHash,
                    tgt.LastModifiedUTC = GETUTCDATE(),
                    tgt.VersionNumber = tgt.VersionNumber + 1

            -- Insert newly recognized events
            WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
                INSERT (
                    EventKey,
                    AccountID,
                    EventCode,
                    PayloadAmount,
                    EventTimestamp,
                    RowHash,
                    CreatedUTC,
                    LastModifiedUTC,
                    VersionNumber
                )
                VALUES (
                    src.EventKey,
                    src.AccountID,
                    src.EventCode,
                    src.PayloadAmount,
                    src.EventTimestamp,
                    src.RowHash,
                    GETUTCDATE(),
                    GETUTCDATE(),
                    1
                );

            -- 4. Mark staging source rows as PROCESSED in the raw ingest ledger
            UPDATE raw
            SET 
                raw.ProcessingStatus = 'PROCESSED',
                raw.ProcessedUTC = GETUTCDATE()
            FROM RawIngest.IncomingEvents raw
            INNER JOIN #StagedEvents stg 
                ON raw.EventKey = stg.EventKey 
               AND raw.AccountID = stg.AccountID
            WHERE stg.DedupRank = 1;

            -- 5. Drop temp table to reclaim tempdb storage immediately
            DROP TABLE #StagedEvents;

            COMMIT TRANSACTION;

            -- 6. Return strictly @@ROWCOUNT to the Flow pipeline variable
            SELECT @@ROWCOUNT AS affected_rows;
            ]]>
        </sql>

        <!-- Verify execution metric in subsequent step -->
        <script id="log_affected_rows" language="go">
            package main
            import (
                "fmt"
                "host/vars"
            )
            func main() {
                count := vars.GetString("TOTAL_ROWS_AFFECTED")
                fmt.Printf("Warehouse consolidation complete. Affected rows reported: %s\n", count)
            }
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Why This Pattern Works in Flow
docs.text:
1. Intelligent Query Detection: Flow strips the leading T-SQL commands (SET NOCOUNT ON, BEGIN TRANSACTION, MERGE, etc.) and detects that the script concludes with a row-returning statement (SELECT @@ROWCOUNT).
  2. Zero In-Memory Payload: Instead of returning 15 million rows across the network into Go's memory, the database handles all merges and updates locally using its storage engine. Only the single scalar row count is returned and stored in TOTAL_ROWS_AFFECTED.
  3. Safe Timeouts: The timeout="45m" attribute ensures that long-running operations are granted appropriate time to complete, while guaranteeing cleanup if a threshold is exceeded.

docs.title: Example 3: High-Performance Cross-Database Bulk Replication (<sql_bulk>)
docs.text:
This example replicates 20 million rows from a PostgreSQL transaction log into a Microsoft SQL Server data lake staging table with minimal transaction logging and optimized batch sizes.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="source_pg" 
                  driver="postgres" 
                  connection_string="postgresql://pg_read:Secret2026@pg-cluster.internal:5432/tx_db?sslmode=require"
                  max_open_conns="30"
                  workload="bulk" />

        <database name="dest_mssql" 
                  driver="sqlserver" 
                  connection_string="sqlserver://sa:Secret2026@mssql-dw.internal:1433?database=StagingLake"
                  max_open_conns="30"
                  workload="bulk" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Stream 20M+ rows directly between engines with zero RAM buffering -->
        <sql_bulk id="replicate_tx_log"
                  db="source_pg"
                  target_db="dest_mssql"
                  target_table="stg_transaction_log"
                  batch_size="25000"
                  tablock="true"
                  check_constraints="false"
                  fire_triggers="false"
                  keep_nulls="true"
                  output_var="REPLICATED_ROW_COUNT">
            SELECT 
                tx_id,
                account_id,
                merchant_id,
                amount,
                currency,
                created_at,
                metadata_json
            FROM transactions.ledger
            WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00Z'
            ORDER BY tx_id ASC;
        </sql_bulk>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Key Performance Features in this Configuration:
docs.text:
• batch_size="25000": Minimizes network round-trip overhead while remaining within server memory buffer limits.
  • tablock="true": Enables table-level locking in SQL Server, switching ingestion from row-by-row logging to fast minimal bulk logging.
  • check_constraints="false": Bypasses constraint validation during the copy to maximize insertion throughput (constraints can be validated in bulk afterward).
  • keep_nulls="true": Ensures explicit NULL values from PostgreSQL are retained and not overwritten by SQL Server column default definitions.

docs.title: 🛠️ Summary Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep Transformations in the Database Engine: When transforming existing database records, use <sql> with in-database DML (MERGE, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, UPDATE ... JOIN) rather than pulling rows into Go to modify them. End your script with SELECT @@ROWCOUNT or SELECT count(*).
  2. Use <sql_bulk> for Table-to-Table Transfers: Whenever data must move between different tables or databases, always prefer <sql_bulk> over custom loops or scripts.
  3. Use Default Streaming in <foreach> for Large Data: If you must loop over query results, rely on <foreach> default streaming mode ($O(1)$ memory). Only add buffer="true" if your loop contains <100,000 rows and you need to release the database connection immediately.
  4. Wrap Multi-Step Sequences in <group transaction="true">: Ensure atomicity and eliminate deadlocks using Flow's automatic dialect-aware savepoint nesting (SAVE TRANSACTION on MSSQL, SAVEPOINT on PostgreSQL/SQLite/MySQL).

docs.title: SQL Bulk Streaming Replication Node (<sql_bulk>) Guide 🚀
docs.text: The <sql_bulk> node is an optimized pipeline streaming primitive that extracts rows from a source SQL query and streams them directly into a target destination table with constant $O(1)$ memory usage. It bypasses intermediate disk files (CSV, Parquet, JSON) and eliminates memory bloat, safely copying tens of millions of records across heterogeneous database engines.

docs.title: 📋 Attribute Specifications
docs.text: Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier across the pipeline. db / database Yes — Source database connection declared in <databases>. target_table / table Yes — Destination table name receiving bulk inserts. target_db / target_database No Source db Destination database connection handle (defaults to source database for intra-database table copies). batch_size No 10000 Number of rows committed per network chunk (recommended: 10000–50000). tablock No true (SQL Server) Acquires table-level lock for minimal transaction logging and maximum insertion speed. check_constraints No false (SQL Server) Validates foreign keys and check constraints during bulk load. Set false for fastest ingestion. fire_triggers No false (SQL Server) Executes insert triggers on the target table during bulk load. Set false for high-throughput ETL. keep_nulls No false (SQL Server) Preserves incoming NULL values instead of replacing them with target column default definitions. timeout No — Bulk copy timeout duration (e.g. 15m, 2h). output_var No — Captures total number of rows streamed to destination into a pipeline variable. condition / cond No — Condition expression required to execute this step. on_error No stop Failure handling strategy: stop, continue, or retry. retry_count No 0 Number of retries on transient connection errors. description No — Human-readable explanation of this bulk replication step.

docs.title: 🎯 High-Performance Tuning Matrix
docs.text: Option / Parameter High-Throughput ETL Setting Safe Audit / Strict Setting Impact & Mechanism batch_size 25000 to 50000 5000 Larger batch sizes amortize network roundtrips. Keep $\le 50000$ to avoid excessive memory buffers on the target server. tablock true false SQL Server: Enables table-level exclusive lock, qualifying the operation for minimal transaction log writes ($10\times$ faster). check_constraints false true When false, SQL Server bypasses checking foreign keys per row during bulk load. Validate constraints in bulk afterward. fire_triggers false true Disabling triggers prevents row-by-row trigger firing overhead during multi-million-row ingestion. keep_nulls true false When true, explicit NULL values from source columns are retained instead of being overwritten by column default constraints.

docs.title: Example 1: Cross-Database Aggregation Streaming (PostgreSQL → SQLite)
docs.text:
Streams aggregated daily orders directly from a production PostgreSQL instance into a local reporting SQLite database:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="oltp_pg" driver="postgres" connection_string="postgresql://app:secret@pg-primary:5432/orders" />
        <database name="reporting_sqlite" driver="sqlite" connection_string="./reporting_daily.db" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Initialize destination schema -->
        <sql id="init_dst_schema" db="reporting_sqlite">
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS daily_sales_summary (
                customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
                total_amount REAL NOT NULL,
                order_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
                summary_date TEXT NOT NULL
            );
        </sql>

        <!-- Stream aggregated rows directly into SQLite -->
        <sql_bulk id="sync_daily_sales"
                  db="oltp_pg"
                  target_db="reporting_sqlite"
                  target_table="daily_sales_summary"
                  batch_size="5000"
                  output_var="ROWS_COPIED">
            SELECT 
                customer_id,
                SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
                COUNT(*) AS order_count,
                CAST(order_date AS TEXT) AS summary_date
            FROM orders
            WHERE order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
            GROUP BY customer_id, order_date;
        </sql_bulk>

        <!-- Validate with assertion -->
        <assert id="verify_replication"
                var="ROWS_COPIED"
                condition="ROWS_COPIED > 0"
                message="Expected at least one daily summary record to be copied." />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Massive 20M+ Row Ingestion into SQL Server with TABLOCK
docs.text:
Transfers millions of transaction records from a transactional PostgreSQL log into a Microsoft SQL Server enterprise staging table:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="source_pg" 
                  driver="postgres" 
                  connection_string="postgresql://etl:Secret2026@pg-cluster.corp:5432/tx_db?sslmode=require"
                  max_open_conns="30"
                  workload="bulk" />

        <database name="dest_mssql" 
                  driver="sqlserver" 
                  connection_string="sqlserver://sa:Secret2026@mssql-dw.corp:1433?database=StagingLake"
                  max_open_conns="30"
                  workload="bulk" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <sql_bulk id="replicate_tx_ledger"
                  db="source_pg"
                  target_db="dest_mssql"
                  target_table="stg_transaction_ledger"
                  batch_size="25000"
                  tablock="true"
                  check_constraints="false"
                  fire_triggers="false"
                  keep_nulls="true"
                  timeout="2h"
                  output_var="TOTAL_REPLICATED">
            SELECT 
                tx_id,
                account_id,
                merchant_id,
                amount,
                currency,
                created_at,
                metadata_json
            FROM transactions.ledger
            WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00Z'
            ORDER BY tx_id ASC;
        </sql_bulk>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: Intra-Database Table-to-Table Streaming (Archival / Staging)
docs.text:
When target_db is omitted, <sql_bulk> automatically reuses the source db connection:

<sql_bulk id="archive_closed_tickets"
          db="crm_database"
          target_table="tickets_archive_2025"
          batch_size="10000"
          output_var="ARCHIVED_COUNT">
    SELECT * 
    FROM tickets 
    WHERE status = 'CLOSED' 
      AND closed_date < '2026-01-01';
</sql_bulk>

docs.title: 🛠️ Workload Comparison: <sql_bulk> vs. <sql> vs. <foreach>
docs.text: Workload Requirement Recommended Node Reason Move rows between different database engines <sql_bulk> Native streaming pipe; zero intermediate files; $O(1)$ RAM usage. Transform data within the same database engine <sql> Keeps data in the database engine (INSERT INTO ... SELECT, MERGE); fastest performance. Call an external REST API or webhook per row <foreach> Iterates row-by-row with streaming cursor; allows dynamic child tasks. Intra-database table replication <sql_bulk> Chunks inserts across batches without transaction log exhaustion.

docs.title: Text Template Generator Node (<template>) Guide 📄
docs.text: The <template> node renders plaintext, configuration files, SQL queries, dynamic emails, or JSON/YAML payloads by leveraging Go's standard text/template engine. It evaluates your active pipeline variables and custom functions, storing the resulting text into a pipeline variable or writing it directly to a disk file.

docs.title: 📋 Attribute Specifications
docs.text:
Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier across the pipeline. into / output_var / var No — Name of pipeline variable to store the rendered text output. file No — File path to write the rendered text directly to disk (or path to external template if used as source). name No Step id Template name assigned during template parsing. engine No text Templating engine: text (Go text/template). mode No — Optional output mode or file permission specification. timeout No — Template rendering deadline duration (e.g. 10s, 1m). condition / cond No — Condition expression required to execute this step. description No — Human-readable explanation of this template step.

[!NOTE] If you are generating HTML content (such as HTML emails or dashboard reports), use <template_html> instead, which provides automatic contextual escaping to prevent security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 📚 Go Standard Library Reference
docs.text:
The <template> node is powered directly by Go's text/template package. The following official documentation covers the full syntax, actions, variables, pipelines, and built-in functions available inside your templates:

Resource URL text/template package docs pkg.go.dev/text/template Built-in template functions pkg.go.dev/text/template#hdr-Functions Template actions reference pkg.go.dev/text/template#hdr-Actions

[!TIP] The full list of built-in functions (and, call, html, index, slice, js, len, not, or, print, printf, println, urlquery, comparison operators) is documented at pkg.go.dev/text/template#hdr-Functions.

docs.title: 🧩 Template Syntax & Expressions
docs.text: The <template> node exposes Go's standard text/template engine syntax:

docs.title: Accessing Pipeline Variables
docs.text:
• Single variable: {{.MY_VAR}} or {{ .MY_VAR }}
  • Nested structures / JSON objects: {{.CONFIG.Database.Host}}
  • Missing variable safety: Empty strings are rendered if a variable does not exist.

docs.title: Conditional Logic
docs.text:
{{if .IS_PRODUCTION}}
Environment: PRODUCTION
Log Level: ERROR
{{else if .IS_STAGING}}
Environment: STAGING
Log Level: DEBUG
{{else}}
Environment: DEVELOPMENT
Log Level: TRACE
{{end}}

docs.title: Looping Over Collections (range)
docs.text:
{{range .USERS}}
User: {{.name}} | Email: {{.email}} | Role: {{.role}}
{{else}}
No users found in active pipeline batch.
{{end}}

docs.title: Built-In Comparison Functions
docs.text:
• eq arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 == arg2
  • ne arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 != arg2
  • lt arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 < arg2
  • le arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 <= arg2
  • gt arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 > arg2
  • ge arg1 arg2: Returns true if arg1 >= arg2
  • and, or, not: Standard boolean operators

docs.title: Example 1: Inline Template into Pipeline Variable
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="USER_NAME" type="string" value="Alice" />
        <variable name="BATCH_ID" type="string" value="B-2026-101" />
        <variable name="STATUS" type="string" value="SUCCESS" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <template id="render_notification" into="SLACK_MESSAGE">
            [ETL Notification]
            Batch: {{.BATCH_ID}}
            Triggered By: {{.USER_NAME}}
            Status: {{.STATUS}}
            Timestamp: 2026-10-11T18:00:00Z
        </template>

        <http_client id="send_slack"
                     url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/T00/B00/X00"
                     method="POST"
                     content_type="application/json">
            {"text": "{{SLACK_MESSAGE}}"}
        </http_client>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Generating a JSON Payload for Webhook Calls
docs.text:
Use <template> to build JSON payloads with dynamic values:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="TRANSACTION_ID" type="string" value="TX-99482" />
        <variable name="AMOUNT" type="float" value="1250.75" />
        <variable name="CURRENCY" type="string" value="USD" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <template id="build_webhook_payload" into="POST_BODY">
            {
                "event": "transaction_processed",
                "transaction_id": "{{.TRANSACTION_ID}}",
                "amount": {{.AMOUNT}},
                "currency": "{{.CURRENCY}}",
                "reconciled": true
            }
        </template>

        <http_client id="post_webhook"
                     url="https://api.partner.com/v1/events"
                     method="POST"
                     content_type="application/json">
            {{POST_BODY}}
        </http_client>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: Dynamic SQL Query Generation
docs.text:
Generate dynamic SQL statements based on runtime parameters and execute them with a downstream <sql> node:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="TARGET_SCHEMA" type="string" value="staging" />
        <variable name="MIN_BALANCE" type="int" value="5000" />
    </variables>

    <databases>
        <database name="app_db" driver="postgres" connection_string="postgresql://app:secret@localhost:5432/appdb" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <template id="build_archive_query" into="ARCHIVE_SQL">
            INSERT INTO {{.TARGET_SCHEMA}}.high_value_accounts (account_id, balance, tier)
            SELECT id, balance, 'GOLD'
            FROM public.accounts
            WHERE balance >= {{.MIN_BALANCE}};
        </template>

        <sql id="execute_archive" db="app_db">
            {{ARCHIVE_SQL}}
        </sql>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 4: Writing Formatted Configuration Files Directly to Disk
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="APP_PORT" type="int" value="8080" />
        <variable name="LOG_LEVEL" type="string" value="INFO" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <template id="generate_env_file" file="./dist/.env">
            PORT={{.APP_PORT}}
            LOG_LEVEL={{.LOG_LEVEL}}
            BUILD_DATE=2026-10-11
        </template>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 🛠️ Summary Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use <template> for Plaintext & Structured Non-HTML Formats: Ideal for SQL, Markdown, CSV, JSON, YAML, and server configuration files.
  2. Switch to <template_html> for HTML Documents: When rendering HTML emails, webpages, or browser dashboards, use <template_html> for automatic contextual XSS protection.
  3. Validate Output with Assertions: Use <assert> on variables populated by <template> to ensure required tokens or valid JSON formatting were produced before proceeding.
  4. Full Syntax Reference: Consult the official Go docs at pkg.go.dev/text/template for the complete action syntax, pipelines, variables, and built-in function list.

docs.title: Overview of the <template> and <template_html> Nodes in Flow
docs.text: The <template> and <template_html> nodes in flow allow you to dynamically generate text, configuration files, emails, or payloads by leveraging Go's powerful text/template engine. The <template> node uses the text/template engine, while the <template_html> node uses the html/template engine, which provides automatic HTML escaping to help prevent XSS vulnerabilities. They evaluate your current pipeline variables and render them into the desired output format, which can then be saved to a variable for use in subsequent pipeline steps.

docs.title: Key Attributes
docs.text:
• id: Unique identifier for the template node.
  • name: (Optional) Name of the template being parsed.
  • file: (Optional) Path to an external template file. If omitted, the node uses inline text.
  • output_var (or var): The variable where the rendered text will be stored.

docs.title: 1. Simple Inline Template
docs.text:
Use the template element to quickly generate text using pipeline variables.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="USER_NAME" type="string" value="Alice" />
        <variable name="ROLE" type="string" value="Admin" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <template id="welcome_msg" output_var="EMAIL_BODY">
            Hello {{.USER_NAME}}, 
            Welcome back! Your current role is: {{.ROLE}}.
        </template>
        <script lang="bash">
            echo "$EMAIL_BODY"
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 2. Loading an External Template File
docs.text:
For larger templates (like HTML emails or complex configurations), you can point the node to an external file.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="REPORT_DATE" type="string" value="2026-08-25" />
        <variable name="TOTAL_SALES" type="float" value="15430.50" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <template id="gen_report" file="templates/monthly_report.tmpl" output_var="HTML_REPORT" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 3. Conditional Rendering
docs.text:
Because it uses Go's text/template, you can use native template logic like if/else directly inside the template.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="IS_PREMIUM" type="bool" value="true" />
        <variable name="USER" type="string" value="Bob" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <template id="promo_msg" output_var="PROMO_TEXT">
            Hi {{.USER}},
            {{if .IS_PREMIUM}}
            Thank you for being a premium subscriber! Here is your 20% discount code.
            {{else}}
            Upgrade to premium today to get exclusive discounts!
            {{end}}
        </template>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 4. Generating a JSON Payload for HTTP POST
docs.text:
A great use case for templates is cleanly generating JSON bodies for subsequent <sql_bulk> calls.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="ORDER_ID" type="int" value="9924" />
        <variable name="STATUS" type="string" value="SHIPPED" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <template id="build_json" output_var="REQ_BODY">
            {
                "order_id": {{.ORDER_ID}},
                "status": "{{.STATUS}}",
                "timestamp": "2026-08-25T18:00:00Z"
            }
        </template>

        <sql_bulk method="POST" uri="https://api.example.com/webhook" content_type="application/json" data="{{REQ_BODY}}" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 5. Dynamic SQL Query Generation
docs.text:
You can render complex SQL statements and pass them into SQL scripts or stream ETL steps.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="TARGET_TABLE" type="string" value="sales_q3" />
        <variable name="MIN_AMOUNT" type="int" value="1000" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <template id="build_sql" output_var="DYNAMIC_SQL">
            SELECT id, amount, customer_id 
            FROM dbo.raw_sales 
            WHERE amount > {{.MIN_AMOUNT}}
            INTO {{.TARGET_TABLE}};
        </template>

        <!-- Execute SQL from variable -->
        <sql db="analytics" var="DYNAMIC_SQL" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 6. Streaming Database Rows to Template and Standard Output (os.stdio)
docs.text: For a comprehensive guide and runnable example demonstrating database streaming row iteration, Go template formatting, and direct printing to os.Stdout (os.stdio), see: * Guide: docs/db_select_template_stdio.md * Example Pipeline: examples/db_select_template_stdio.xml

docs.title: Context-Aware HTML Template Node (<template_html>) Guide 🌐
docs.text: The <template_html> node (alias: <html_template>) renders dynamic HTML reports, emails, dashboard components, and status pages using Go's standard html/template package. Unlike standard plaintext templating, html/template is context-aware: it automatically inspects the surrounding HTML syntax (tags, attributes, JavaScript, CSS, URIs) and applies the precise escaping required to prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and code injection vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 📋 Attribute Specifications
docs.text: Attribute Required Default Description id Yes — Unique step identifier across the pipeline. into / output_var / var No — Pipeline variable name to store the rendered HTML document or fragment. file No — File path to write the rendered HTML directly to disk (e.g. reports/summary.html). name No Step id Template name assigned during template parsing. engine No html Templating engine: html (Go html/template). mode No — Optional file permission or output formatting specification. timeout No — Template rendering deadline duration (e.g. 10s, 1m). condition / cond No — Condition expression required to execute this step. description No — Human-readable explanation of this HTML template step.

docs.title: 📚 Go Standard Library Reference
docs.text:
The <template_html> node is powered directly by Go's html/template package, which shares the same syntax as text/template but adds context-aware HTML escaping. Official documentation:

Resource URL html/template package docs pkg.go.dev/html/template text/template syntax reference pkg.go.dev/text/template Built-in template functions pkg.go.dev/text/template#hdr-Functions Template actions reference pkg.go.dev/text/template#hdr-Actions Security model pkg.go.dev/html/template#hdr-Security_Model

[!TIP] html/template is a drop-in superset of text/template. Any valid text/template syntax also works in <template_html> — the only difference is the automatic context-sensitive escaping applied at render time.

docs.title: 🛡️ Context-Aware Escaping Explained
docs.text:
Go's html/template parses the full HTML document grammar. When variables are interpolated, it applies different sanitizers depending on the exact context:

Injection Context Template Snippet Automatic Sanitization Applied HTML Body <p>{{.MESSAGE}}</p> Converts <, >, &, ", and ' to HTML character entities (<, >, &). HTML Attribute <input value="{{.NAME}}"> Quotes and escapes special characters so malicious input cannot break out of attributes. Hyperlink / URL <a href="{{.LINK}}"> Validates URI schemes; filters dangerous prefixes like javascript:. Inline JavaScript <script>var id = {{.USER_ID}};</script> Encodes values into valid JSON/JavaScript literals, preventing script breakout attacks. CSS Style Block <div style="color: {{.COLOR}}"> Strips invalid CSS properties and prevents style-based script injection.

docs.title: Example 1: Executive ETL Execution Summary Report (HTML File)
docs.text:
Generates a standalone, styled HTML execution dashboard and writes it directly to disk:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="PIPELINE_NAME" type="string" value="Nightly Customer Ledger Sync" />
        <variable name="RECORDS_PROCESSED" type="int" value="142580" />
        <variable name="EXECUTION_STATUS" type="string" value="SUCCESS" />
        <variable name="DURATION" type="string" value="1m 42s" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <template_html id="render_dashboard" file="./reports/latest_execution.html">
            <![CDATA[
            <!DOCTYPE html>
            <html lang="en">
            <head>
                <meta charset="UTF-8">
                <title>ETL Execution Report - {{.PIPELINE_NAME}}</title>
                <style>
                    body { font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif; background: #0f172a; color: #f8fafc; padding: 2rem; }
                    .card { background: #1e293b; border-radius: 12px; padding: 24px; max-width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; box-shadow: 0 4px 6px -1px rgba(0,0,0,0.3); border: 1px solid #334155; }
                    .badge { display: inline-block; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: 9999px; font-weight: bold; font-size: 12px; }
                    .badge-success { background: #065f46; color: #34d399; }
                    .stat { margin: 12px 0; font-size: 14px; color: #94a3b8; }
                    .stat strong { color: #f8fafc; }
                </style>
            </head>
            <body>
                <div class="card">
                    <h2>{{.PIPELINE_NAME}}</h2>
                    <div class="stat">Status: <span class="badge badge-success">{{.EXECUTION_STATUS}}</span></div>
                    <div class="stat">Records Processed: <strong>{{.RECORDS_PROCESSED}}</strong></div>
                    <div class="stat">Duration: <strong>{{.DURATION}}</strong></div>
                    <div class="stat">Generated: <strong>2026-10-11T18:00:00Z</strong></div>
                </div>
            </body>
            </html>
            ]]>
        </template_html>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Tabular Report Iterating Over Extracted Database Records
docs.text:
Combines <sql> extraction with <template_html> collection iteration ({{range ...}}):

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <databases>
        <database name="sales_db" driver="sqlite" connection_string="./sales.db" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Extract top sales representatives into JSON array variable -->
        <sql id="fetch_top_sales" db="sales_db" output_var="TOP_REPS">
            SELECT rep_name, region, quarterly_sales
            FROM representatives
            WHERE quarterly_sales >= 100000
            ORDER BY quarterly_sales DESC;
        </sql>

        <!-- Render safe HTML email fragment -->
        <template_html id="format_email_table" into="EMAIL_TABLE_HTML">
            <![CDATA[
            <table border="1" cellpadding="8" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%;">
                <tr style="background-color: #2563eb; color: white;">
                    <th>Representative</th>
                    <th>Region</th>
                    <th>Quarterly Sales</th>
                </tr>
                {{range .TOP_REPS}}
                <tr>
                    <td>{{.rep_name}}</td>
                    <td>{{.region}}</td>
                    <td align="right">${{.quarterly_sales}}</td>
                </tr>
                {{else}}
                <tr>
                    <td colspan="3" align="center">No qualifying sales records found.</td>
                </tr>
                {{end}}
            </table>
            ]]>
        </template_html>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: Contextual XSS Protection Demonstration
docs.text:
Demonstrating that malicious inputs like <script>alert('xss')</script> are safely escaped into harmless entities without manual developer sanitization:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <!-- Untrusted user input containing malicious markup -->
        <variable name="USER_INPUT" type="string" value="<script>alert('pwnd')</script>" />
        <variable name="PROFILE_URL" type="string" value="javascript:stealTokens()" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <template_html id="safe_rendering" into="SAFE_HTML">
            <div>
                <!-- Automatically escaped to <script>alert('pwnd')</script> -->
                <p>Welcome, {{.USER_INPUT}}!</p>

                <!-- Automatically neutralized because scheme is javascript: -->
                <a href="{{.PROFILE_URL}}">View Profile</a>
            </div>
        </template_html>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 🛠️ Summary Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always Use <template_html> for Web / Email Output: Never use plaintext <template> for content rendered in web browsers or email clients.
  2. Enclose Markup in CDATA: Wrap HTML template blocks containing <, >, or & within <![CDATA[ ... ]]> to prevent XML parser syntax errors.
  3. Use into for Variables, file for Disk Output: Specify into="VAR_NAME" if passing HTML to <http_client> (e.g. SendGrid or SES API), or file="path/to/file.html" to save directly to disk.
  4. Full Syntax & Security Reference: See the official Go docs at pkg.go.dev/html/template for the complete escaping model, supported contexts, and security guarantees.

docs.title: Pipeline Variables (<variable>) & Registry Guide
docs.text: The <variable> element initializes a named pipeline variable within the top-level <variables> container. Flow provides a high-performance, thread-safe variable registry (*flow.Registry) that enables dynamic parameterization of SQL queries, file paths, connection strings, HTTP endpoints, loop drivers, and cross-runtime script execution.

docs.title: 1. Syntax & Attribute Reference
docs.text:
Pipeline variables are declared inside the <variables> collection at the beginning of the pipeline:

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables description="Global pipeline configuration and state variables">
        <variable id="var-batch-id" name="BatchID" type="int" value="1001" description="Current batch identifier" />
        <variable id="var-target-table" name="TargetTable" type="string" value="daily_sales" description="Destination table" />
        <variable id="var-is-prod" name="IsProduction" type="bool" value="true" description="Environment switch" />
    </variables>
    <!-- flow nodes -->
</pipeline>

docs.title: <variables> Container Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Mandatory Default Description description No "" Optional human-readable description of the variables collection.

docs.title: <variable> Element Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Mandatory Default Description name Yes — Unique variable name. Used for interpolation (e.g., {{VariableName}}), registry lookups, and OS environment variable exports. value Yes — Initial scalar string value assigned to the variable. Evaluated and converted according to type. type No string Data type for parsing and internal representation. Supported types: string, int, integer, bool, boolean, float, double, float64, datetime, date. id No "" Optional unique identifier for the variable definition element. description No "" Optional human-readable description of the variable's purpose, origin, or usage.

docs.title: 2. Supported Data Types & Value Parsing
docs.text:
When initializing variables via XML, Flow parses string values into typed native representations:

Type Name Aliases Description Parsing Rules & Examples string — (Default) Scalar text / string Preserves literal text as entered: value="production", value="C:\Data\Reports". int integer 64-bit signed integer (int64) Parses base-10 integer numbers: value="5000", value="-42". bool boolean Boolean flag Case-insensitive boolean parsing: true, false, 1, 0, t, f, TRUE, FALSE. float double, float64 64-bit floating point (float64) Parses IEEE 754 floating point numbers: value="99.95", value="-0.0042". datetime — ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 Timestamp Parses standard timestamp formats (e.g. 2026-01-15T08:30:00Z, 2026-01-15 08:30:00). date — Calendar Date Parses calendar dates formatted as YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. 2026-01-15).

docs.title: 3. Variable Scopes & Concurrency Model
docs.text:
Variables are managed by a centralized, thread-safe registry (*flow.Registry). Their scoping behavior adapts automatically based on the execution context:

flowchart TD
    Root["Root Pipeline Registry<br/><code>[BatchID: 1001] [TargetTable: 'sales'] [Env: 'prod']</code>"]

    Root -->|Sequential Blocks: <flow>, <group>| Shared["Shared Registry Mutex<br/>• Immediate read/write visibility<br/>• Step B immediately sees Step A's updates"]

    Root -->|Parallel Blocks: <parallel>| Workers["Thread Snapshots / Clones<br/>• Worker 0: Local copy + <code>_THREAD_ID=0</code><br/>• Worker 1: Local copy + <code>_THREAD_ID=1</code>"]

    Workers -->|Worker Completion| Merge["Dirty Merge & Conflict Resolution<br/>• Clean variables merged back to parent<br/>• Colliding edits namespaced to <code>WORKER_<id>_<key></code>"]

docs.title: Sequential Execution (Default)
docs.text: In root <flow>, <preflight>, and <group> blocks: - All steps share a single synchronized registry. - Variable reads and mutations (output_var, into) are immediately visible to all subsequent steps.

docs.title: Parallel Execution (<parallel>)
docs.text: When running concurrent branches inside <parallel> blocks: - Flow snapshots (deep-clones) the variable registry for each concurrent worker thread. - Automatically injects an integer _THREAD_ID variable (0, 1, 2, ...) into each worker's local scope. - Workers mutate their private copy without blocking or corrupting other threads. - Upon worker completion, only mutated ("dirty") variables are merged back into the parent registry. - If two or more parallel workers mutate the same key with differing values, Flow applies automatic conflict resolution, namespacing colliding entries to WORKER_<id>_<key> to prevent race conditions and stale overwrites.

docs.title: 4. Variable Interpolation Syntax
docs.text: Flow supports mustache-style double curly brace interpolation: {{VariableName}}. Placeholders are resolved case-insensitively at runtime across pipeline components:

docs.title: 1. SQL Statements & Queries (<sql>, <sql_bulk>)
docs.text:
<sql id="QueryWithLimit" db="reporting_db">
    SELECT order_id, customer_name, total_amount
    FROM {{TargetTable}}
    WHERE order_date >= '{{StartDate}}'
    LIMIT {{BatchLimit}};
</sql>

docs.title: 2. Database Connection Strings (<database>)
docs.text:
<database name="dynamic_db" driver="postgres"
          connection_string="host={{DB_HOST}} port={{DB_PORT}} user={{DB_USER}} password={{DB_PASS}} dbname={{DB_NAME}}" />

docs.title: 3. File & Directory Paths (<file_read>, <file_save>, <excel_read>, <excel_write>)
docs.text: <file_read id="LoadBatchFile" path="{{StorageDir}}/incoming/{{BatchID}}_{{BatchDate}}.csv" into="RawCsvData" />

docs.title: 4. HTTP Client URLs & Headers (<http_client>)
docs.text:
<http_client id="SyncWebhook" method="POST"
             url="https://api.internal.net/v1/orders/{{OrderID}}"
             headers="Authorization: Bearer {{API_TOKEN}}; Content-Type: application/json"
             body="{{PayloadJson}}" />

docs.title: 5. Conditional Expressions (<if>, <group>, <while>, <assert>)
docs.text: <assert id="VerifyTotal" var="RecordCount" equals="{{ExpectedCount}}" message="Row count mismatch!" />

docs.title: 5. Setting & Mutating Variables at Runtime
docs.text:
Variables can be dynamically updated by any pipeline node supporting output capture:

Pipeline Node Output Attribute Capture Behavior <sql> output_var / into Captures single scalar result (single row/col) or tab-delimited text. <script> output_var Captures trimmed standard output (stdout) produced by script execution. <http_client> into / output_var Captures HTTP response body. status_into captures status code. <template> into / output_var Captures rendered Go text/template output. <template_html> into / output_var Captures rendered Go html/template (context-aware escaped) output. <file_read> into / output_var Reads entire file content into string variable. <excel_read> output_var / into Captures parsed Excel table rows formatted as delimited or JSON data. <json_path> into / output_var Extracts specific value, object, or array matching JSONPath expression. <yaml_path> into / output_var Evaluates path query against YAML data and stores extracted value. <xml_xpath> into / output_var Evaluates XPath expression on XML document and stores result. <kv> into / output_var Retrieves stored value for given key from Key-Value store.

docs.title: 6. Automatic Loop Injections
docs.text: Looping constructs automatically bind contextual iteration variables:

docs.title: <foreach>
docs.text:
Iterates over rows returned by a SQL driver query: - LOOP_INDEX: 0-indexed loop iteration counter (0, 1, 2, ...). - Column Bindings: Every column returned by the driver query is automatically injected into the iteration registry under three casing formats: 1. Exact Case: as defined in SQL SELECT (e.g. CustomerId). 2. Lowercase: customerid. 3. Uppercase: CUSTOMERID.

<foreach id="ProcessAccounts" db="app_db">
    SELECT account_id, org_name, status FROM accounts WHERE active = 1;

    <!-- Automatically available: {{account_id}}, {{org_name}}, {{status}}, {{LOOP_INDEX}} -->
    <sql id="LogAccount" db="audit_db">
        INSERT INTO audit_log (account_id, message, iteration)
        VALUES ({{account_id}}, 'Processed {{org_name}}', {{LOOP_INDEX}});
    </sql>
</foreach>

docs.title: <while>
docs.text: Iterates while condition remains true: - WHILE_INDEX: 0-indexed iteration counter (0, 1, 2, ...).

docs.title: 7. Consuming Variables in Script Nodes
docs.text: Flow passes all registry variables into script runtimes:

docs.title: 1. Embedded Go Interpreter (yaegi)
docs.text:
Import "host/vars" to access strongly-typed getter functions: 

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "host/vars"
)

func main() {
    batchId := vars.GetInt("BatchID")
    table   := vars.GetString("TargetTable")
    isProd  := vars.GetBool("IsProduction")
    fmt.Printf("Batch %d targeting %s (Prod=%t)\n", batchId, table, isProd)
}

Available "host/vars" Methods: - vars.Get(name string) interface{} - vars.GetString(name string) string - vars.GetInt(name string) int - vars.GetBool(name string) bool - vars.GetFloat(name string) float64

docs.title: 2. C# (dotnet-script / csx)
docs.text:
Variables are exposed as OS environment variables: 

using System;

string targetTable = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("TargetTable");
string rawBatchId  = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("BatchID");
Console.WriteLine($"Running for {targetTable} (Batch {rawBatchId})");

docs.title: 3. PowerShell (pwsh / powershell)
docs.text:
Variables are accessible via the $env: drive: 

Write-Host "Processing table: $env:TargetTable"
Write-Host "Batch ID: $env:BatchID"

docs.title: 4. Linux Bash & POSIX Shell (bash / shell)
docs.text:
Variables are exported into the child process environment: 

echo "Processing table: ${TargetTable}"
echo "Current environment: ${IsProduction}"

docs.title: 8. Variable Precedence & Overrides
docs.text:
When a variable name is defined in multiple places, Flow evaluates them in strict order of precedence (highest wins):

flowchart BT
    subgraph Precedence ["Variable Precedence Hierarchy (Highest to Lowest)"]
        Base["4. Base Pipeline Declarations (<variables>)<br/><i>Lowest Precedence</i>"]
        Config["3. External Config Overlays (-config override.xml)"]
        CLI["2. Command-Line Overrides (-vars 'Key=Val')"]
        Runtime["1. Dynamic Step Mutations (output_var, into, foreach)<br/><b>Highest Precedence</b>"]

        Base --> Config
        Config --> CLI
        CLI --> Runtime
    end
  1. Base Pipeline XML: Initial values declared in <variables>.
  2. External Config File (-config override.xml): Overrides matching variable keys before execution starts.
  3. CLI Arguments (-vars "Key=Value,Count=50"): Overrides matching variable keys at launch.
  4. Runtime Node Mutations (output_var, into): Overwrites registry entries during pipeline execution.

docs.title: Example 1: Multi-Type Variable Initialization & Validation
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables description="ETL batch parameters and thresholds">
        <variable id="v1" name="BatchID" type="int" value="42" description="Current execution batch ID" />
        <variable id="v2" name="BatchDate" type="date" value="2026-10-11" description="Processing calendar date" />
        <variable id="v3" name="ThresholdRate" type="float" value="0.95" description="Quality score threshold" />
        <variable id="v4" name="DryRun" type="bool" value="false" description="Toggle commit vs rollback" />
        <variable id="v5" name="ReportTitle" type="string" value="Monthly Aggregates" description="Report heading" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <assert id="CheckBatchID" var="BatchID" equals="42" message="BatchID was not initialized properly" />
        <assert id="CheckDryRun" var="DryRun" equals="false" message="DryRun flag must be false" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Dynamic SQL Scalar Capture & Conditional Branching
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="PendingCount" type="int" value="0" description="Number of pending records" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <!-- Capture scalar count into PendingCount -->
        <sql id="CountPending" db="warehouse_db" output_var="PendingCount">
            SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staging_events WHERE status = 'PENDING';
        </sql>

        <!-- Execute group only when pending rows exist -->
        <group id="ProcessBatchGroup" if_var="PendingCount" if_val="0" equals="false">
            <sql id="ProcessPending" db="warehouse_db">
                UPDATE staging_events 
                SET status = 'PROCESSED', processed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
                WHERE status = 'PENDING';
            </sql>
        </group>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: Cross-Language Variable Passing (Go to PowerShell to SQL)
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="SourceDir" type="string" value="./data/incoming" />
        <variable name="FileCount" type="int" value="0" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <!-- Step 1: PowerShell counts files and writes to stdout -->
        <script id="CountIncomingFiles" language="powershell" output_var="FileCount">
            $files = Get-ChildItem -Path $env:SourceDir -Filter *.csv
            Write-Host -NoNewline $files.Count
        </script>

        <!-- Step 2: Go script evaluates threshold -->
        <script id="EvaluateThreshold" language="go" output_var="EvaluationStatus">
            package main
            import (
                "fmt"
                "host/vars"
            )
            func main() {
                count := vars.GetInt("FileCount")
                if count > 0 {
                    fmt.Print("READY")
                } else {
                    fmt.Print("EMPTY")
                }
            }
        </script>

        <!-- Step 3: SQL records the audit log using interpolated variables -->
        <sql id="RecordAudit" db="audit_db">
            INSERT INTO etl_audit (source_directory, files_found, status)
            VALUES ('{{SourceDir}}', {{FileCount}}, '{{EvaluationStatus}}');
        </sql>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 4: Thread-Isolated Variables in <parallel> Workers
docs.text:
<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="BaseOutputDir" type="string" value="./output" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <parallel id="ConcurrentShardProcess">
            <!-- Worker 0: _THREAD_ID is 0 -->
            <script id="ProcessShard0" language="go">
                package main
                import (
                    "fmt"
                    "host/vars"
                )
                func main() {
                    thread := vars.GetInt("_THREAD_ID")
                    dir := vars.GetString("BaseOutputDir")
                    fmt.Printf("Worker %d writing to %s/shard_%d\n", thread, dir, thread)
                }
            </script>

            <!-- Worker 1: _THREAD_ID is 1 -->
            <script id="ProcessShard1" language="go">
                package main
                import (
                    "fmt"
                    "host/vars"
                )
                func main() {
                    thread := vars.GetInt("_THREAD_ID")
                    dir := vars.GetString("BaseOutputDir")
                    fmt.Printf("Worker %d writing to %s/shard_%d\n", thread, dir, thread)
                }
            </script>
        </parallel>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Flow Variable Management & Usage Guide
docs.text: Flow supports dynamic environment variables stored in a thread-safe registry (*flow.Registry). These variables enable you to parameterize your SQL queries, loop drivers, streaming configurations, and dynamic Go scripts.

docs.title: 1. Variable Hierarchy & Scope
docs.text:
Variables are kept in a single unified registry, but their behavior and scope change depending on the pipeline execution tree block:

Scope Context Behavior Global / Registry Sequential execution Read and write actions are immediate and shared. Scripts executing in a sequence (inside a standard group or root block) can read variables written by preceding scripts. Thread-Isolated <parallel> blocks When running concurrent branches, Flow snapshots (clones) the registry's variables for each worker thread, injecting a unique thread-specific _THREAD_ID variable (starting from 0). Only variables mutated by a worker (dirty variables) are merged back to the parent. If multiple parallel workers mutate the same key, a conflict-resolution routine namespaces them into WORKER_<id>_<key> to prevent race conditions or overwriting concurrent edits with stale values.

docs.title: SQL Queries (Variable Interpolation)
docs.text:
For SQL nodes, variables are dynamically interpolated before execution using double curly brace placeholders: {{VarName}}.

<sql id="QueryWithLimit" db="app_db">
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' LIMIT {{MaxLimit}};
</sql>

docs.title: Go Scripts (Yaegi vars Exports)
docs.text:
Inside dynamic Go scripts, variables are retrieved using the built-in host package "host/vars". The package exposes typed getters:

  • vars.Get(name string) interface{}
  • vars.GetString(name string) string
  • vars.GetInt(name string) int
  • vars.GetBool(name string) bool
  • vars.GetFloat(name string) float64
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "host/vars"
)

func main() {
    threshold := vars.GetInt("Threshold")
    table := vars.GetString("TargetTable")
    fmt.Printf("Processing %s with threshold: %d\n", table, threshold)
}

docs.title: C# Scripts (dotnet-script / csx Environment Variables)
docs.text:
Inside dynamic C# scripts, all registry variables are loaded directly into the OS process environment. You can retrieve them using:

  • Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("VariableName")
using System;
string targetTable = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("TargetTable");
Console.WriteLine($"Writing to {targetTable}");

docs.title: SQL Queries (output_var)
docs.text:
To capture a value returned from a SQL query, use the output_var attribute. * If the SQL query returns a single row with a single column, output_var stores that value. * Otherwise, it captures the entire tab-separated results block.

<sql id="GetMaxID" db="app_db" output_var="LastProcessedID">
    SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) FROM logs;
</sql>

docs.title: Go Scripts (output_var / Stdout Capture)
docs.text:
Because the Yaegi host bindings do not expose a variable mutation method, you write values to variables by printing them to stdout. The output_var attribute will capture the printed console output and store it as a string variable.

<script id="CalculateStats" language="go" output_var="ResultScore">
    package main
    import "fmt"
    func main() {
        score := 98.4
        // Captured directly by "ResultScore"
        fmt.Printf("%.1f", score)
    }
</script>

docs.title: C# Scripts (output_var / Stdout Capture)
docs.text:
Similar to Go and shell scripts, dotnet-script outputs to stdout are captured by the output_var attribute and stored back into the pipeline variable registry.

<script id="CsharpCalc" language="dotnet-script" output_var="ResultSum">
    using System;
    int a = 10;
    int b = 20;
    Console.Write(a + b); // Captured directly by "ResultSum"
</script>

docs.title: 4. Loops (<foreach>)
docs.text:
When iterating over records using a <foreach> block, the loop driver query binds the following variables automatically for each iteration:

  • LOOP_INDEX: The current 0-indexed loop iteration index (integer).
  • Columns: The values of the current row are bound to variables matching the column names. To prevent casing issues, the engine binds them in three casings:
    1. Exact Case (e.g. UserId)
    2. Lowercase (e.g. userid)
    3. Uppercase (e.g. USERID)
<foreach id="IterateUsers" db="app_db" var="UserId">
    SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE active = 1;

    <!-- Each iteration binds "id", "username", "email", and "LOOP_INDEX" -->
    <sql id="ProcessUser" db="app_db">
        INSERT INTO user_audit (user_id, action) 
        VALUES ({{id}}, 'Processed iteration {{LOOP_INDEX}}');
    </sql>
</foreach>

docs.title: Example A: Exporting Multiple Parameters (Comma-Separated Output)
docs.text:
When you need to output multiple distinct values from a script to be consumed as separate parameters in a subsequent step, you can format the output as a delimited string and parse it inside the next Go script.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <flow>
