        <!-- Step 1: Export a delimited config from Go -->
        <script id="GenerateParams" language="go" output_var="MultiParams">
            package main
            import "fmt"
            func main() {
                env := "production"
                retries := 5
                timeout := 30
                fmt.Printf("%s,%d,%d", env, retries, timeout)
            }
        </script>

        <!-- Step 2: Consume and split parameters inside another Go script -->
        <script id="UseParams" language="go">
            package main
            import (
                "fmt"
                "strings"
                "strconv"
                "host/vars"
            )
            func main() {
                raw := vars.GetString("MultiParams")
                parts := strings.Split(raw, ",")
                if len(parts) == 3 {
                    env := parts[0]
                    retries, _ := strconv.Atoi(parts[1])
                    timeout, _ := strconv.Atoi(parts[2])
                    fmt.Printf("Env: %s, Retries: %d, Timeout: %d\n", env, retries, timeout)
                }
            }
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example B: Passing JSON Output Between Scripts
docs.text:
For complex, structured data, you can output a JSON string, capture it, and parse it back into typed structs in subsequent dynamic Go scripts.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <flow>
        <!-- Step 1: Query database config details, formatting output as JSON -->
        <script id="FetchServiceConfig" language="go" output_var="ServiceJSON">
            package main
            import (
                "encoding/json"
                "fmt"
            )
            type ConnectionDetails struct {
                Host string `json:"host"`
                Port int    `json:"port"`
                SSL  bool   `json:"ssl"`
            }
            func main() {
                cfg := ConnectionDetails{
                    Host: "db-replica.internal",
                    Port: 5432,
                    SSL:  true,
                }
                bytes, _ := json.Marshal(cfg)
                fmt.Println(string(bytes))
            }
        </script>

        <!-- Step 2: Unmarshal and utilize the JSON payload in a subsequent step -->
        <script id="ConnectToService" language="go">
            package main
            import (
                "encoding/json"
                "fmt"
                "host/vars"
            )
            type ConnectionDetails struct {
                Host string `json:"host"`
                Port int    `json:"port"`
                SSL  bool   `json:"ssl"`
            }
            func main() {
                jsonStr := vars.GetString("ServiceJSON")
                var cfg ConnectionDetails
                if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(jsonStr), &cfg); err != nil {
                    fmt.Printf("Failed to unmarshal config: %v\n", err)
                    return
                }
                fmt.Printf("Successfully established connection to %s:%d (SSL: %t)\n", cfg.Host, cfg.Port, cfg.SSL)
            }
        </script>
    </flow>

</pipeline>

docs.title: Example C: Inter-operating Go and C# Scripts
docs.text:
You can easily pass state between dynamic Go interpreter scripts and C# process-executed scripts using variables.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="Threshold" type="int" value="42" />
    </variables>
    <flow>
        <!-- Step 1: Read Threshold variable in C#, run calculations, and store output -->
        <script id="CsharpStep" language="dotnet-script" output_var="CS_Result">
            using System;
            string rawThreshold = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("Threshold");
            if (int.TryParse(rawThreshold, out int threshold)) {
                Console.Write($"Threshold was {threshold}, calculated result is {threshold * 2}");
            }
        </script>

        <!-- Step 2: Use the C# result inside a Go script -->
        <script id="GoStep" language="go">
            package main
            import (
                "fmt"
                "host/vars"
            )
            func main() {
                csVal := vars.GetString("CS_Result")
                fmt.Printf("Go received from C#: %s\n", csVal)
            }
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Conditional Iteration: <while>
docs.text:
The <while> component repeats execution of its inner child steps as long as an evaluation condition or variable comparison remains true. It is designed for polling asynchronous database jobs, paginated REST API extractions, wait-and-retry workflows, and multi-pass batching loops.

<while> includes a built-in safety ceiling (max_iterations, default 1000) to protect against runaway infinite loops and automatically injects a zero-based iteration tracker {{WHILE_INDEX}}.

docs.title: Architecture & Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Start([Enter <while> Loop]) --> InitIndex["Initialize WHILE_INDEX = 0"]
    InitIndex --> CheckLimit{"WHILE_INDEX >= max_iterations?<br/>(default: 1000)"}

    CheckLimit -- "Yes (Safety Guard)" --> Tripwire[/"Error / Terminate Loop<br/>(Loop limit exceeded)"/]
    CheckLimit -- "No" --> EvalCond{"Evaluate Loop Condition<br/>condition or var == equals"}

    EvalCond -- "False / Not Equal" --> Exit([Loop Terminates Successfully])
    EvalCond -- "True / Equal" --> ExecChildren["Execute Child Steps Sequentially"]

    ExecChildren --> Incr["Increment WHILE_INDEX = WHILE_INDEX + 1"]
    Incr --> CheckLimit

docs.title: Attribute Reference
docs.text: Attribute Type Default Mandatory Description id string (generated) No Unique identifier for the while loop step. var string "" Conditional Name of the pipeline variable monitored for equality (e.g. JobStatus). if_var string "" No Alias for var. equals string "" Conditional Loop continues while var equals this string or value (e.g. RUNNING or true). val / value string "" No Aliases for equals. if_val / if_equals string "" No Aliases for equals. condition string "" Conditional Expression evaluated before each iteration (e.g. ne .Status "DONE" or lt .PAGE_COUNT 10). cond string "" No Alias for condition. max_iterations positiveInteger 1000 No Infinite loop guard ceiling. Pipeline halts if iterations reach this threshold. max_loops positiveInteger 1000 No Alias for max_iterations. timeout string (none) No Optional timeout duration for the total while block (e.g. 5m, 30s). on_error string stop No Error handling policy for inner child failures: stop, continue, or retry. retry_count integer 0 No Number of retries permitted per child failure before applying on_error. description string "" No Human-readable explanation of the loop's purpose.

docs.title: 1. Loop Control Modes
docs.text:
<while> supports two distinct condition styles:

  • Variable Equality Mode (var + equals): Monitors a specific variable and repeats as long as its value matches equals. 

    <while id="poll_sync" var="SYNC_STATUS" equals="IN_PROGRESS" max_iterations="30">
    <!-- Child steps query status and update SYNC_STATUS -->
</while>

  • Expression Condition Mode (condition): Evaluates boolean or comparison expressions dynamically before each pass. 

    <while id="page_iterator" condition="and (eq .HAS_MORE \"true\") (lt .CURRENT_PAGE 50)" max_iterations="50">
    <!-- Child steps fetch next page and update HAS_MORE -->
</while>

docs.title: 2. Built-in WHILE_INDEX Variable
docs.text:
On every pass through the loop, the engine injects a zero-based iteration index named WHILE_INDEX: - Iteration 1: {{WHILE_INDEX}} = 0 - Iteration 2: {{WHILE_INDEX}} = 1 - Iteration 3: {{WHILE_INDEX}} = 2

Child steps, Go scripts (vars.GetInt("WHILE_INDEX")), SQL queries, and log statements can access {{WHILE_INDEX}} directly.

docs.title: 3. Infinite Loop Protection (max_iterations)
docs.text: To prevent unbounded resource consumption or runaway API costs, <while> defaults to a maximum ceiling of 1,000 iterations. If the loop condition remains true after reaching max_iterations, execution halts immediately with an explanatory error.

docs.title: 4. Pacing & Delay
docs.text:
Most polling workflows require pauses between iterations. You can introduce delays using an embedded <script language="go"> with time.Sleep(...): 

<script id="poll_delay" language="go">
    package main
    import "time"
    func main() {
        time.Sleep(3 * time.Second)
    }
</script>

docs.title: Example 1: Asynchronous Database Job Polling (MSSQL)
docs.text:
Poll the status of a long-running SQL Server Agent or stored procedure task until completion.

<pipeline description="Poll MSSQL background job status"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="JobStatus" type="string" value="RUNNING" />
        <variable name="TargetJobId" type="string" value="JOB_2026_0981" />
    </variables>

    <databases>
        <database name="primary_db" 
                  connection_string="sqlserver://SRV01:1433?database=AppDB&integrated+security=true" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Loop while JobStatus is RUNNING, max 30 attempts (approx 60s total) -->
        <while id="poll_mssql_job" var="JobStatus" equals="RUNNING" max_iterations="30"
               description="Wait for background batch procedure to complete">

            <!-- Step 1: Wait 2 seconds between polling checks -->
            <script id="sleep_step" language="go">
                package main
                import "time"
                func main() {
                    time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)
                }
            </script>

            <!-- Step 2: Query database and update JobStatus output variable -->
            <sql id="fetch_status" db="primary_db" output_var="JobStatus">
                SELECT TOP 1 [status]
                FROM dbo.async_tasks WITH (NOLOCK)
                WHERE task_id = '{{TargetJobId}}';
            </sql>

            <!-- Step 3: Log progress using WHILE_INDEX -->
            <script id="log_attempt" language="go">
                package main
                import (
                    "fmt"
                    "host/vars"
                )
                func main() {
                    idx := vars.GetInt("WHILE_INDEX")
                    status := vars.GetString("JobStatus")
                    fmt.Printf("[Attempt #%d] Current Job Status: %s\n", idx+1, status)
                }
            </script>
        </while>

        <!-- Final verification gate -->
        <assert id="verify_success" var="JobStatus" equals="SUCCESS" message="Background job failed or timed out" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 2: Paginated REST API Extraction
docs.text:
Retrieve records page by page from an external REST API until has_more returns false or the max page limit is reached.

<pipeline description="Paginated REST API Data Extraction"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="PAGE_NUM" type="int" value="1" />
        <variable name="HAS_MORE" type="string" value="true" />
        <variable name="API_RESPONSE" type="string" value="" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <while id="paginate_api" var="HAS_MORE" equals="true" max_iterations="100"
               description="Fetch user pages until has_more is false">

            <!-- Request current page -->
            <http_client id="fetch_page" 
                         url="https://api.example.com/v2/events?page={{PAGE_NUM}}&limit=100" 
                         method="GET" 
                         into="API_RESPONSE" />

            <!-- Extract has_more boolean flag -->
            <json_path id="check_has_more" source="var" var="API_RESPONSE" query="$.pagination.has_more" into="HAS_MORE" />

            <!-- Append page payload to raw log file -->
            <file_save id="append_page" file="./data/events_feed.jsonl" source="var" var="API_RESPONSE" append="true" />

            <!-- Increment PAGE_NUM for the next pass -->
            <script id="incr_page" language="go">
                package main
                import "host/vars"
                func main() {
                    current := vars.GetInt("PAGE_NUM")
                    vars.Set("PAGE_NUM", current+1)
                }
            </script>
        </while>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 3: External Service Readiness & Health Check
docs.text:
Wait for a remote container or database service to become healthy with exponential backoff.

<pipeline description="Wait for remote service readiness"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="IS_READY" type="string" value="false" />
        <variable name="HTTP_STATUS" type="int" value="0" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <while id="wait_for_health" var="IS_READY" equals="false" max_iterations="20" timeout="5m">
            <!-- Ping health endpoint -->
            <http_client id="check_health" url="http://microservice.internal/healthz" method="GET" status_into="HTTP_STATUS" on_error="continue" />

            <!-- If HTTP 200, mark IS_READY to true to exit loop -->
            <if id="eval_health" condition="eq .HTTP_STATUS 200">
                <then>
                    <variable id="set_ready" name="IS_READY" value="true" />
                </then>
                <else>
                    <!-- Backoff pause before re-checking -->
                    <script id="backoff_sleep" language="go">
                        package main
                        import "time"
                        func main() {
                            time.Sleep(3 * time.Second)
                        }
                    </script>
                </else>
            </if>
        </while>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 4: Chunked Queue Consumer & Staging Purge
docs.text:
Process a work queue in batches until no pending records remain in the queue table.

<pipeline description="Drain work queue table in batches"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="PENDING_COUNT" type="int" value="1" />
    </variables>

    <databases>
        <database name="queue_db" connection_string="postgres://app:secret@localhost:5432/appdb?sslmode=disable" />
    </databases>

    <flow>
        <!-- Loop while there are pending tasks (PENDING_COUNT > 0) -->
        <while id="drain_queue" condition="gt .PENDING_COUNT 0" max_iterations="500">
            <!-- Process 1000 items in a transaction -->
            <group id="batch_worker" transaction="true" db="queue_db">
                <sql id="archive_batch" db="queue_db">
                    WITH batch AS (
                        SELECT id FROM processing_queue 
                        WHERE status = 'PENDING' 
                        LIMIT 1000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
                    )
                    UPDATE processing_queue q
                    SET status = 'PROCESSED', processed_at = NOW()
                    FROM batch
                    WHERE q.id = batch.id;
                </sql>

                <!-- Check remaining count -->
                <sql id="count_remaining" db="queue_db" output_var="PENDING_COUNT">
                    SELECT COUNT(*) AS PENDING_COUNT FROM processing_queue WHERE status = 'PENDING';
                </sql>
            </group>
        </while>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Example 5: Multi-Stage Pipeline State Polling with <assert>
docs.text:
Poll a cloud export or machine learning job until status reaches either COMPLETED or FAILED, using assertions to catch fatal errors.

<pipeline description="Cloud export job status monitor"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="JOB_ID" type="string" value="EXP_8829" />
        <variable name="STATUS" type="string" value="PENDING" />
        <variable name="RESPONSE" type="string" value="" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <!-- Keep polling while STATUS is PENDING or PROCESSING -->
        <while id="monitor_cloud_job" condition="or (eq .STATUS \"PENDING\") (eq .STATUS \"PROCESSING\")" max_iterations="40">
            <script id="wait_5s" language="go">
                package main
                import "time"
                func main() {
                    time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)
                }
            </script>

            <http_client id="get_status" url="https://cloud.example.com/api/jobs/{{JOB_ID}}" method="GET" into="RESPONSE" />
            <json_path id="parse_status" source="var" var="RESPONSE" query="$.job.status" into="STATUS" />
        </while>

        <!-- Guarantee final status was COMPLETED -->
        <assert id="assert_job_finished_ok" var="STATUS" equals="COMPLETED" 
                message="Export job did not complete successfully" on_failure="halt" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: Best Practices & Troubleshooting
docs.text:
[!TIP] Always Include a Delay: In polling loops, always add a <script> sleep step between iterations to prevent aggressive CPU spinning or API rate-limit penalties (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests).

[!IMPORTANT] Update Monitored Variables: Ensure that at least one child step within the <while> block alters the monitored variable (output_var="...", <variable>, or vars.Set(...)). If the variable is never updated, the loop will run until max_iterations is hit.

[!WARNING] Set Realistic max_iterations: Tailor max_iterations to your operational expectations (e.g. max_iterations="30" with a 2-second sleep gives a 60-second window). Relying on the 1000 default for a 5-second polling loop could keep a blocked pipeline open for over an hour.

docs.title: Guide: XML XPath Extraction Node (<xml_xpath>)
docs.text: The <xml_xpath> node provides advanced XML querying and parsing functionality within the Flow Pipeline Engine. Powered by xmlquery, it allows users to execute standard XPath expressions over XML files or environment variables and extract matched elements into plaintext, raw XML, or JSON formats.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
• id (string, optional): Unique step identifier.
  • file (string, optional): Path to the source XML file on disk. Supports dynamic path interpolation (e.g. {{xml_path}}).
  • var (string, optional): Variable key containing the raw XML string payload to parse.
  • xpath (string, optional): The XPath query expression to execute.
  • mode (string, optional): Output serialization format:
  • "text" (default): Returns the inner text of matched elements, joined by newlines.
  • "xml": Returns raw XML strings (including element tags and nested content), joined by newlines.
  • "json_array": Returns matched elements or text contents serialized into a single JSON array list of strings.
  • output_var (string, required): Variable key to store the resulting output.

[!NOTE] If the xpath attribute is omitted, the engine automatically extracts the XPath query from the inner body text of the element.

docs.title: 💡 Practical Examples
docs.text: The following examples demonstrate common workflows using <xml_xpath>.

docs.title: Example 1: Extracting Inner Text (Default "text" Mode)
docs.text:
Retrieves the text inside targeted tags and joins the results together with newlines.

Source XML File (inventory.xml): 

<inventory>
  <item id="101">
    <name>Wireless Mouse</name>
    <category>Peripherals</category>
  </item>
  <item id="102">
    <name>Mechanical Keyboard</name>
    <category>Peripherals</category>
  </item>
</inventory>

XML Pipeline Definition: 

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
  <variables>
    <variable name="xml_file" type="string" value="inventory.xml" />
  </variables>
<flow>
  <!-- Query names in default plaintext join mode -->
  <xml_xpath id="get_names" file="{{xml_file}}" xpath="//item/name" output_var="item_names" />
  </flow>
</pipeline>

Resulting Output (item_names): 

Wireless Mouse
Mechanical Keyboard

docs.title: Example 2: Extracting Outer XML Elements (mode="xml")
docs.text:
Selects whole node trees and outputs them with their XML tags preserved.

XML Pipeline Definition: 

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
  <flow>
    <!-- Select the full raw XML structures for all items -->
    <xml_xpath id="get_raw_items" 
               file="inventory.xml" 
               xpath="//item" 
               mode="xml" 
               output_var="raw_items" />
  </flow>
</pipeline>

Resulting Output (raw_items): 

<item id="101"><name>Wireless Mouse</name><category>Peripherals</category></item>
<item id="102"><name>Mechanical Keyboard</name><category>Peripherals</category></item>

docs.title: Example 3: Exporting to JSON Lists (mode="json_array")
docs.text:
Extracts attribute values or text nodes and packs them into a marshalled JSON string array.

XML Pipeline Definition: 

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
  <flow>
    <!-- Query the 'id' attribute values of all items and output as JSON list -->
    <xml_xpath id="get_ids" 
               file="inventory.xml" 
               xpath="//item/@id" 
               mode="json_array" 
               output_var="item_ids_json" />
  </flow>
</pipeline>

Resulting Output (item_ids_json): 

["101", "102"]

docs.title: Example 4: XPath Expressions with Variable Interpolation
docs.text:
Leverages runtime pipeline variables inside the XPath query itself for dynamic filtering.

XML Pipeline Definition: 

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
  <variables>
    <variable name="target_id" type="string" value="102" />
  </variables>
  <flow>
    <!-- Query item name dynamically using target_id variable -->
    <xml_xpath id="get_target_name" 
               file="inventory.xml" 
               xpath="//item[@id='{{target_id}}']/name" 
               output_var="target_name" />
  </flow>
</pipeline>

Resulting Output (target_name): 

Mechanical Keyboard

docs.title: Example 5: Inline Query Specifications (Inner Text)
docs.text:
Allows writing long, complex, or formatted XPath expressions cleanly inside the node body instead of cluttering attributes.

XML Pipeline Definition: 

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
  <variables>
    <variable name="raw_xml" type="string" value="<root><user role='admin'>Alice</user><user role='user'>Bob</user></root>" />
  </variables>

  <!-- Executes query written directly within body text -->
  <xml_xpath id="query_admins" var="raw_xml" output_var="admin_users">
    //user[@role='admin']
  </xml_xpath>
  </flow>
</pipeline>

Resulting Output (admin_users): 

Alice

docs.title: Overview of the <yaml_path> Node in Flow
docs.text: The <yaml_path> node in flow enables evaluating path queries against raw YAML content loaded from disk files or stored inside pipeline variables. It converts YAML structures into normalized JSON in memory and evaluates path expressions, writing the output back to downstream pipeline variables.

docs.title: Key Attributes
docs.text:
• file: (Optional) Path to a .yaml or .yml file on disk. Supports {{VarName}} variable interpolation.
  • var: (Optional) Pipeline environment variable containing raw YAML text.
  • path / yamlpath: (Optional) The path query expression to evaluate. Alternatively, the path expression can be written inside the element body.
  • mode: (Optional) Format of the extracted output:
  • value (Default): Returns scalar text or line-separated value matches.
  • json: Returns extracted sub-objects as a formatted JSON string.
  • json_array: Serializes all matched nodes into a JSON array string.
  • yaml: Serializes matched nodes back into clean YAML block format.
  • output_var / out_var: Target pipeline environment variable where extracted results will be saved.

docs.title: 1. Extracting a Database Host from a Configuration File
docs.text:
Load a service configuration file and extract a scalar database connection string.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="CONFIG_FILE" type="string" value="./config/app.yaml" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <!-- Extract the database host string into variable DB_HOST -->
        <yaml_path 
            file="{{CONFIG_FILE}}" 
            path="$.database.connection.host" 
            output_var="DB_HOST" />

        <script lang="bash">
            echo "Connecting to database at: $DB_HOST"
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 2. Extracting Nested Objects as JSON (mode="json")
docs.text:
Extract a sub-map or configuration block from a YAML file directly into a JSON string to pass into an HTTP client node.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <flow>
        <!-- Extract the entire telemetry configuration block as JSON -->
        <yaml_path 
            file="./config/services.yaml" 
            path="$.telemetry.metrics" 
            mode="json" 
            output_var="METRICS_CONFIG_JSON" />

        <sql_bulk 
            method="POST" 
            uri="[https://api.example.com/v1/config](https://api.example.com/v1/config)" 
            content_type="application/json" 
            data="{{METRICS_CONFIG_JSON}}" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 3. Multi-Line Body Expression with Variable Interpolation
docs.text:
Place dynamic or complex path queries directly inside the element body using template variable substitution.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <variables>
        <variable name="ENVIRONMENT" type="string" value="production" />
    </variables>

    <flow>
        <file_read file="./config/deployments.yaml" output_var="MANIFEST_YAML" />

        <!-- Filter deployment settings based on pipeline environment -->
        <yaml_path var="MANIFEST_YAML" output_var="ACTIVE_REPLICAS">
            $.environments[?(@.name == '{{ENVIRONMENT}}')].replicaCount
        </yaml_path>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 4. Extracting Kubernetes Container Images (mode="json_array")
docs.text:
Extract a list of container images from a Kubernetes manifest file as a clean JSON array string.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <flow>
        <!-- Query all container images across all specs -->
        <yaml_path 
            file="./k8s/deployment.yaml" 
            mode="json_array" 
            output_var="CONTAINER_IMAGES">
            $.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image
        </yaml_path>

        <script lang="bash">
            echo "Deployed Images Array: $CONTAINER_IMAGES"
        </script>
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 5. Re-serializing Matched Nodes to YAML (mode="yaml")
docs.text:
Extract a sub-section of a larger YAML document and output it formatted as valid YAML for writing to disk.

<pipeline xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/flow/main/xsd/pipeline.xsd">
    <flow>
        <file_read file="./config/cluster.yaml" output_var="FULL_CLUSTER_YAML" />

        <!-- Extract storage spec back out as pure YAML -->
        <yaml_path 
            var="FULL_CLUSTER_YAML" 
            path="$.cluster.storage" 
            mode="yaml" 
            output_var="STORAGE_YAML" />

        <!-- Write the isolated storage configuration to a new file -->
        <file_save file="./output/storage_spec.yaml" var="STORAGE_YAML" />
    </flow>
</pipeline>

docs.title: 📚 etl — Automation & ETL Summary
docs.text: Flow is a Go-based, enterprise-grade ETL orchestration engine and pipeline executor driven by XML pipeline definitions and an optional HTMX visual web UI. It bridges declarative pipeline design with execution, supporting multi-dialect relational and key-value database operations, parallel processing, embedded scripting (via the Yaegi Go interpreter), multi-sink event telemetry, and automated diagram generation.

docs.title: Core System Architecture & CLI Interface
docs.text:
The application functions as a zero-dependency binary CLI runner and interactive server. Pipeline behavior, inputs, and environments are managed through CLI flags, XML configurations, and variable injection mechanisms.

Flag / Parameter Type Default Automation & ETL Purpose -builder bool false Launches the interactive HTMX web server backed by flow_builder.db for visual pipeline design. -builder-port int 0 Specifies the listening port for the visual builder web server (default 0 for dynamic ephemeral port). -file string scripts.xml Specifies the primary XML configuration file containing pipeline nodes, variables, and DB definitions. -config string "" Secondary XML configuration file path for environment-specific overrides (DBs, variables, preflight nodes). -vars string "" Comma-separated key=value runtime variable overrides (e.g., -vars "TargetTable=foo,Limit=100"). -options string "" XML file containing pre-configured default CLI flag options (applies options only if not explicitly set on CLI). -validate bool false Runs non-executing validation passes (XSD schema validation and semantic AST check). -preflight bool false Executes preflight validation nodes only (e.g., source file checks, staging table verification) without running main flow. -format string csv Execution result output renderer (json, jsonpretty, text, markdown, csv, stream). -xslt / -out string "" Path to XSLT stylesheet and output file to transform pipeline XML and inject generated Mermaid diagrams.

docs.title: Orchestration & Control Flow Primitives
docs.text:
Flow builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) from XML definitions, supporting complex execution topologies, branching logic, and streaming data movement.

AST Element Execution Semantics & Capabilities <script> Executes script logic in specified languages (e.g., Go via Yaegi, SQL) with optional target database row-streaming (target_db). <sql> / <sql_bulk> Executes single or bulk SQL operations against registered relational or K/V database connections. <group> Groups related execution steps into a logical sequential unit. <parallel> Executes child pipeline nodes concurrently across threads and joins them at completion. <if> Evaluates dynamic conditions (condition string or var == equals) to branch into <then> or <else> blocks. <foreach> / <loop> / <while> Iterates over dataset records or variable criteria, executing child nodes per row until completion. <preflight> Dedicated execution phase intended for schema sanity checks, target table truncations, and prerequisite validation.

docs.title: Multi-Dialect Database Support & Telemetry Sinks
docs.text:
Flow provides abstract database handling across both traditional relational engines and Key-Value stores. Connection strings support dynamic variable template resolution (e.g., {{log_db_cs}}).

Storage Engine / Dialect Parameter Placeholder Special SQL Dialect Handling PostgreSQL $1, $2, $3 Auto-detected from postgres:// or dbname= connection strings. Microsoft SQL Server @p1, @p2, @p3 Auto-detects driver; prepends dbo. to table names if schema is omitted. Oracle :1, :2, :3 Auto-detected via oracle:// or driver reflection (godror, oracle). MySQL / SQLite / K/V ?, ?, ? Standard positional binding; handles K/V lookup state and SQL dialects.

docs.title: Operational Logging & Audit Schemas
docs.text:
When a log_db database connection is configured, Flow automatically logs telemetry via DatabaseSink into two standardized tables:

  1. pipeline_runs (Pipeline-Level Summary Log):

  2. Fields: run_id, file_path, config_path, status, started_at, finished_at, duration_ms, task_count, error_class, error_message.

  3. pipeline_events (Step-Level Event Audit):

  4. Fields: run_id, execution_id, sequence_num, occurred_at, event_type, node_kind, node_id, status, error_message, rows_read, rows_written, rows_affected.

docs.title: Automation Lifecycle, Validation, and Documentation
docs.text:
[XML Script + Option Profile] ➔ [XSD & AST Validation] ➔ [Preflight Nodes] ➔ [Parallel / Sequential Execution] ➔ [Multi-Sink Audit Logging]
                                                                                          │
                                                                                          ├──> Console Output (JSON/CSV/Markdown)
                                                                                          └──> Mermaid Diagram & XSLT Report

  • Configuration Inheritance: Variables and database configurations are merged hierarchically: Base XML (scripts.xml) < Override XML (-config) < CLI parameters (-vars). Connection string templates (e.g., {{db_password}}) are iteratively expanded up to 3 depth levels.

  • Pre-Execution Safety: -validate verifies both XSD structural compliance (using xmllint) and semantic AST validity (checking node linkages and database references) without touching data stores.

  • Live Observability: Using -format stream, execution progress is piped in real-time to stdout as RFC3339-timestamped CSV event streams alongside standard DatabaseSink persistence.

  • Visual Documentation Generation: Flow parses pipeline XML directly into Mermaid.js TD flowcharts, capturing variable tables, database connections, conditional branches, loops, and parallel join nodes. The XSLT 3.0 transformation engine (helium/xslt3) can merge this flowchart directly into transformed reports or automated documentation packages.

docs.title: Single-File Cryptography: Combining Encryption & Digital Signatures
docs.text: This guide explains how to combine digital signatures and AES-256-GCM encryption into a single, unified file for execution with flow.exe / flow. It details the cryptographic envelope formats, explains how to avoid common configuration pitfalls (such as detached signature confusion), and provides end-to-end walkthroughs for Windows (PowerShell / Windows Cert Store) and Linux / macOS (OpenSSL / Bash / zsh), including generating self-signed certificates with both OpenSSL and crypto_tool.

docs.title: 1. Unified Envelopes vs. Detached Signatures
docs.text:
go-flow and its companion tool crypto_tool support two distinct distribution models for signed and encrypted pipelines:

Model Files on Disk File Reference in options.xml How Verification Operates Detached Signature 2 Filespipeline.xml.encpipeline.xml.enc.sig Points to the payload (pipeline.xml.enc).Never point to the .sig file! flow.exe auto-discovers <file>.sig, verifies the detached signature against the payload, and then decrypts the payload. Unified Single File(Recommended) 1 Filepipeline.xml.sec Points directly to the single unified package (pipeline.xml.sec). Both the cryptographic signature and the encrypted payload are packaged together in a single self-contained envelope. 
flowchart TD
    subgraph Detached["Detached Signature (2 Files on Disk)"]
        D1["pipeline.xml.enc (Payload)"]
        D2["pipeline.xml.enc.sig (Detached Signature)"]
        D1 -.->|"flow auto-detects companion"| D2
    end

    subgraph Unified["Unified Package (1 Single File on Disk)"]
        U1["pipeline.xml.sec<br/>FLOWSIGNED:v1:FORMAT:<Signature>:<FLOWENC Ciphertext>"]
    end

docs.title: The Common Pitfall: Pointing to .sig Files Directly
docs.text:
A common mistake when using detached signatures is configuring options.xml or -file to point directly to the .sig file:

<!-- INCORRECT: Pointing directly to a detached signature file -->
<file>.\deploy\pipeline.xml.enc.sig</file>
<encrypted>true</encrypted>
<secure-key>SecretKey</secure-key>

When this happens: 1. pipeline.xml.enc.sig contains only an ASCII signature header (e.g. FLOWSIG:v1:OPENSSL-RSA-SHA256:...). 2. Because <encrypted>true</encrypted> is set, flow attempts to decrypt the ASCII signature bytes as if they were AES-256 ciphertext. 3. AES-GCM authentication tag validation fails immediately with: 

failed to decrypt resource: decryption failed: invalid key or tampered ciphertext
4. Resolution: Point <file> to pipeline.xml.enc (which lets flow auto-detect pipeline.xml.enc.sig), or use a unified single-file envelope as described below.

docs.title: 2. The Two Unified Architectures
docs.text: go-flow supports two single-file patterns:

docs.title: Architecture A: Encrypt-then-Sign (FLOWSIGNED:v1: with -wrap) — Recommended
docs.text:
In this pattern, the plaintext pipeline XML is encrypted first, and the resulting ciphertext is signed and packaged into a self-contained envelope using crypto_tool -wrap.

flowchart LR
    A["Plaintext XML"] -->|"1. AES-256-GCM<br/>(crypto_tool -action encrypt)"| B["Ciphertext<br/>(FLOWENC:v1:...)"]
    B -->|"2. Digital Sign & Wrap<br/>(crypto_tool -action sign -wrap)"| C["Unified Package<br/>(FLOWSIGNED:v1:...)"]

docs.title: Envelope Anatomy:
docs.text: FLOWSIGNED:v1:<FORMAT>:<base64(DigitalSignature)>:<base64(FLOWENC:v1:Salt:Nonce:Ciphertext:Tag)>

docs.title: Why This Is Recommended:
docs.text:
• Zero Attack Surface: flow validates the digital signature over the ciphertext first. Untrusted or tampered payloads are rejected before decryption keys are touched or decrypted data is loaded into memory.
  • Transparent Decryption: Once the outer signature passes verification, the engine automatically extracts the inner FLOWENC:v1: payload and decrypts it using the provided -key-file, -secure-key, or FLOW_SECURE_KEY.

docs.title: Architecture B: Sign-then-Encrypt (FLOWENC:v1: containing FLOWSIGNED:v1:)
docs.text:
In this pattern, the plaintext XML is signed into a FLOWSIGNED:v1: envelope first, and then the entire signed package is encrypted into an outer FLOWENC:v1: payload.

flowchart LR
    A["Plaintext XML"] -->|"1. Digital Sign & Wrap<br/>(crypto_tool -action sign -wrap)"| B["Signed Envelope<br/>(FLOWSIGNED:v1:...)"]
    B -->|"2. AES-256-GCM<br/>(crypto_tool -action encrypt)"| C["Encrypted Package<br/>(FLOWENC:v1:...)"]

docs.title: Envelope Anatomy:
docs.text: FLOWENC:v1:<base64(AES-256-GCM-Ciphertext-Enclosing-FLOWSIGNED-Envelope)>

docs.title: When to Use:
docs.text:
• Signer Privacy: In regulated or multi-tenant environments where the identity of the signer, certificate metadata, and signature algorithms must remain strictly confidential from external observers.
  • Lifecycle: flow decrypts the outer ciphertext first, detects that the inner content is a FLOWSIGNED:v1: envelope, and immediately verifies the digital signature before executing the pipeline.

docs.title: 3. End-to-End Walkthrough: Windows (PowerShell & Certificates)
docs.text: This walkthrough demonstrates creating and running a unified single-file pipeline on Windows using standard PowerShell and an X.509 code signing certificate.

docs.title: Prerequisites & Example Setup
docs.text: Assume the following directory structure: * C:\etl\pipelines\ — Source directory containing raw pipeline definitions. * C:\etl\deploy\ — Production deployment directory. * C:\certs\ — Secure certificate and key storage.

docs.title: Step 1: Exporting or Generating Certificate & Private Key on Windows
Option 1: Export Public Certificate from Windows Certificate Store
docs.text:
# Locate your code-signing certificate thumbprint
Get-ChildItem -Path Cert:\CurrentUser\My -CodeSigningCert

# Export the public certificate in X.509 format (.cer)
$cert = Get-Item Cert:\CurrentUser\My\3F4B8C1E0A2D3E4F5A6B7C8D9E0F1A2B3C4D5E6F
Export-Certificate -Cert $cert -FilePath C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.cer

docs.title: Option 2: Export Private Key via PFX & Convert to PEM
docs.text:
If the private key is marked exportable, export the PFX and extract the PEM private key: 

# Export PFX with a temporary export passphrase
$pwd = ConvertTo-SecureString -String "ExportTempPass123!" -AsPlainText -Force
Export-PfxCertificate -Cert $cert -FilePath C:\certs\enterprise_signer.pfx -Password $pwd

# Extract the private key as standard PEM using OpenSSL
openssl pkcs12 -in C:\certs\enterprise_signer.pfx -nocerts -out C:\certs\enterprise_signer_key.pem -nodes
openssl pkcs12 -in C:\certs\enterprise_signer.pfx -clcerts -nokeys -out C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.pem

docs.title: Option 3: Generate New Keypair & Self-Signed Certificate Directly with crypto_tool
docs.text:
If you do not have an existing enterprise certificate authority, generate an RSA keypair and self-signed X.509 certificate directly (no external OpenSSL required): 

.\crypto_tool.exe -action gen-keypair `
    -keypair-type rsa `
    -bits 4096 `
    -out-priv C:\certs\enterprise_signer_key.pem `
    -out-pub C:\certs\enterprise_signer_pub.pem `
    -out-cert C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.pem `
    -cn "Enterprise ETL Pipeline Signer"

docs.title: Step 2: Encrypt the Plaintext Pipeline
docs.text:
Given a plaintext pipeline C:\etl\pipelines\daily_sales_etl.xml, encrypt it using AES-256-GCM.

[!TIP] To prevent secrets from appearing in process listings, supply the encryption passphrase via -key-file or the FLOW_SECURE_KEY environment variable.

# Store key securely in a key file
Set-Content -Path C:\certs\encryption.key -Value "EnterpriseSecretPassphrase2026!" -NoNewline

# Encrypt pipeline to text-armored ciphertext
.\crypto_tool.exe -action encrypt `
    -in C:\etl\pipelines\daily_sales_etl.xml `
    -out C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl.enc `
    -key-file C:\certs\encryption.key

docs.title: Step 3: Sign and Wrap into a Single Unified File
docs.text:
Sign the encrypted file with your code signing certificate and include the -wrap flag:

.\crypto_tool.exe -action sign `
    -in C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl.enc `
    -out C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl_unified.sec `
    -private-key C:\certs\enterprise_signer_key.pem `
    -cert C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.pem `
    -sig-type openssl `
    -wrap

Output: 

Successfully signed C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl.enc -> C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl_unified.sec (format: OPENSSL-RSA-SHA256)

The resulting file daily_sales_etl_unified.sec is a single text-armored file containing both the digital signature and the encrypted payload. No separate .sig file is generated or needed.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure options.xml for Unified Single-File Execution
docs.text:
Create your execution options file (C:\etl\options\daily_sales_options.xml):

<flow_cli_options xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/go-flow/main/xsd/options.xsd">
    <options>
        <!-- Single unified file containing signature + encrypted payload -->
        <file>C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl_unified.sec</file>
        <format>stream</format>

        <!-- Security flags -->
        <verify-signature>true</verify-signature>
        <encrypted>true</encrypted>

        <!-- Verification certificate (X.509 .cer or .pem) -->
        <cert>C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.pem</cert>

        <!-- Decryption key file (avoids storing passwords in XML) -->
        <key-file>C:\certs\encryption.key</key-file>
    </options>
</flow_cli_options>

[!NOTE] <cert> supports both PEM certificates (.pem, .crt) and raw Windows binary DER certificates (.cer).

If your signing certificate was issued by an internal Enterprise Root CA, you can also supply <ca-cert> to validate the complete chain of trust:

<ca-cert>C:\certs\enterprise_root_ca.cer</ca-cert>

docs.title: Step 5: Execute the Pipeline on Windows with flow.exe
docs.text: Execute the pipeline using either the options file or direct CLI flags:

docs.title: Method A: Using options.xml
docs.text: .\flow.exe -options C:\etl\options\daily_sales_options.xml

docs.title: Method B: Using Direct Command Line Flags
docs.text:
.\flow.exe `
    -file C:\etl\deploy\daily_sales_etl_unified.sec `
    -cert C:\certs\enterprise_code_signer.pem `
    -key-file C:\certs\encryption.key `
    -verify-signature `
    -encrypted `
    -format stream

docs.title: 4. End-to-End Walkthrough: Linux & macOS (Bash / zsh)
docs.text: This walkthrough demonstrates creating self-signed certificates, signing, encrypting, and running a unified single-file pipeline on Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, Alpine) and macOS.

docs.title: Prerequisites & Example Setup
docs.text:
Assume standard POSIX production paths: * /opt/etl/pipelines/ — Source directory containing raw pipeline definitions. * /opt/etl/deploy/ — Production deployment directory. * /etc/ssl/flow/ (or ~/.certs/) — Restricted certificate and key storage.

mkdir -p /opt/etl/pipelines /opt/etl/deploy /opt/etl/options /etc/ssl/flow
chmod 700 /etc/ssl/flow

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Self-Signed Certificate & Keypair
docs.text: You can generate your self-signed code-signing certificate using standard OpenSSL or directly with crypto_tool.

docs.title: Option A: Using OpenSSL (Standard on Linux & macOS)
docs.text:
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key and self-signed X.509 certificate in a single command:

# Generate private key and self-signed certificate (valid for 365 days)
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 \
    -keyout /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem \
    -out /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem \
    -days 365 \
    -nodes \
    -subj "/C=US/ST=California/L=San Francisco/O=Enterprise ETL/CN=Flow Pipeline Signer"

# Restrict private key permissions (owner read-only)
chmod 600 /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem
chmod 644 /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem

For modern Elliptic Curve (ECDSA P-256) instead of RSA: 

openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 \
    -keyout /etc/ssl/flow/flow_ecdsa_key.pem \
    -out /etc/ssl/flow/flow_ecdsa_cert.pem \
    -days 365 \
    -nodes \
    -subj "/CN=Flow ECDSA Pipeline Signer"

chmod 600 /etc/ssl/flow/flow_ecdsa_key.pem

docs.title: Option B: Using crypto_tool Directly (Pure Go — Zero External Dependencies)
docs.text:
If OpenSSL is not installed (e.g. minimal Docker containers, Alpine Linux, or lightweight VMs), use crypto_tool's built-in gen-keypair action:

# Generate 4096-bit RSA keypair and self-signed X.509 certificate
./crypto_tool -action gen-keypair \
    -keypair-type rsa \
    -bits 4096 \
    -out-priv /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem \
    -out-pub /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_pub.pem \
    -out-cert /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem \
    -cn "Flow Pipeline Signer"

# Secure permissions
chmod 600 /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem
chmod 644 /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_pub.pem

Output: 

Successfully generated rsa keypair:
  Private key: /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem
  Public key:  /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_pub.pem
  Certificate: /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Secure Symmetric Encryption Key File
docs.text:
Store your AES-256 encryption passphrase in a dedicated key file with restricted POSIX permissions (0600) so it cannot be read by other system users:

# Create key file with restricted permissions
echo -n "EnterpriseSecretPassphrase2026!" > /etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key
chmod 600 /etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key

docs.title: Step 3: Encrypt the Pipeline (AES-256-GCM)
docs.text:
Encrypt the raw pipeline definition /opt/etl/pipelines/daily_sales_etl.xml:

./crypto_tool -action encrypt \
    -in /opt/etl/pipelines/daily_sales_etl.xml \
    -out /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl.enc \
    -key-file /etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key

docs.title: Step 4: Sign and Wrap into a Unified File (.sec)
docs.text:
Digitally sign the encrypted ciphertext using your private key and wrap it into a single FLOWSIGNED:v1:... envelope:

./crypto_tool -action sign \
    -in /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl.enc \
    -out /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec \
    -priv /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem \
    -cert /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem \
    -sig-type openssl \
    -wrap

Output: 

Successfully signed /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl.enc -> /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec (format: OPENSSL-RSA-SHA256)

docs.title: Streamlined Alternative: Single-Line Unix Pipe (Zero Intermediate Files)
docs.text:
Because crypto_tool supports standard input/output (-in - and -out -), you can encrypt and sign in a single command pipeline without writing daily_sales_etl.enc to disk:

./crypto_tool -action encrypt -in /opt/etl/pipelines/daily_sales_etl.xml -key-file /etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key -out - | \
./crypto_tool -action sign -in - -priv /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_key.pem -cert /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem -wrap -out /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec

docs.title: Step 5: Verify the Unified File Manually (Optional)
docs.text:
Verify that the unified .sec file passes cryptographic validation against the self-signed certificate:

./crypto_tool -action verify \
    -in /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec \
    -cert /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem

Output: 

Signature VALID (OPENSSL via RSA-SHA256, Signer: Flow Pipeline Signer)

docs.title: Step 6: Execute on Linux / macOS with flow
Method A: Using Command Line Flags
docs.text:
./flow \
    -file /opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec \
    -cert /etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem \
    -key-file /etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key \
    -verify-signature \
    -encrypted \
    -format stream

docs.title: Method B: Using Options File (/opt/etl/options/daily_sales_options.xml)
docs.text:
<flow_cli_options xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etl-madness/go-flow/main/xsd/options.xsd">
    <options>
        <file>/opt/etl/deploy/daily_sales_etl_unified.sec</file>
        <format>stream</format>
        <verify-signature>true</verify-signature>
        <encrypted>true</encrypted>
        <cert>/etc/ssl/flow/flow_signer_cert.pem</cert>
        <key-file>/etc/ssl/flow/encryption.key</key-file>
    </options>
</flow_cli_options>

./flow -options /opt/etl/options/daily_sales_options.xml

docs.title: 5. Execution Lifecycle & Verification Output
docs.text:
When flow executes a unified package, it performs verification and decryption in sequential order:

[FLOW] Verifying digital signature on resource "daily_sales_etl_unified.sec"...
[FLOW] Signature verified successfully. Signer: "Flow Pipeline Signer" (Algorithm: OPENSSL-RSA-SHA256).
[FLOW] Decrypting AES-256-GCM payload using provided security key...
[FLOW] Decryption successful.
[FLOW] Parsing pipeline XML schema and abstract syntax tree...
[FLOW] Pipeline initialized: "daily_sales_pipeline". Executing nodes...

If any tampering occurs: * Altered Ciphertext or Signature: 

Error reading script file: digital signature verification failed for resource "...daily_sales_etl_unified.sec": RSA signature verification failed
* Tampered Certificate or Untrusted Signer: 
Error reading script file: certificate verification failed: certificate signed by unknown authority
* Tampered Payload inside Decryption Stage: 
Error reading script file: decryption failed: invalid key or tampered ciphertext

docs.title: 6. Summary Cheat Sheet (Windows, Linux, macOS)
docs.text: Task Windows (PowerShell) Linux / macOS (Bash / zsh) Create Self-Signed Certificate (OpenSSL) openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=Signer" openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=Signer" Create Self-Signed Certificate (crypto_tool) .\crypto_tool.exe -action gen-keypair -bits 4096 -out-priv key.pem -out-cert cert.pem -cn "Signer" ./crypto_tool -action gen-keypair -bits 4096 -out-priv key.pem -out-cert cert.pem -cn "Signer" Create Secure Key File Set-Content -Path secret.key -Value "Passphrase" -NoNewline echo -n "Passphrase" > secret.key && chmod 600 secret.key 1. Encrypt XML .\crypto_tool.exe -action encrypt -in job.xml -out job.enc -key-file secret.key ./crypto_tool -action encrypt -in job.xml -out job.enc -key-file secret.key 2. Sign & Wrap (Single File) .\crypto_tool.exe -action sign -in job.enc -out job.sec -priv key.pem -cert cert.pem -wrap ./crypto_tool -action sign -in job.enc -out job.sec -priv key.pem -cert cert.pem -wrap 3. Streamlined Piped Single-Step .\crypto_tool.exe -action encrypt -in job.xml -key-file secret.key -out - \| .\crypto_tool.exe -action sign -in - -priv key.pem -cert cert.pem -wrap -out job.sec ./crypto_tool -action encrypt -in job.xml -key-file secret.key -out - \| ./crypto_tool -action sign -in - -priv key.pem -cert cert.pem -wrap -out job.sec 4. Verify Manually .\crypto_tool.exe -action verify -in job.sec -cert cert.pem ./crypto_tool -action verify -in job.sec -cert cert.pem 5. Run Single File with Flow .\flow.exe -file job.sec -cert cert.pem -key-file secret.key -verify-signature -encrypted ./flow -file job.sec -cert cert.pem -key-file secret.key -verify-signature -encrypted 6. Run via Options File .\flow.exe -options options.xml ./flow -options options.xml

docs.title: Compilation, Git Workflow & Build Options Guide
docs.text:
Complete Reference for Cloning, Building, Cross-Compiling, and Packaging the go-flow Ecosystem Binaries Covered: flow (flow.exe), crypto_tool (crypto_tool.exe), db_importer (db_importer.exe) Go Toolchain: Go 1.26.5+ | Pure-Go Static Compilation: Supported (CGO_ENABLED=0)

This guide provides step-by-step instructions for cloning the Flow (go-flow) repository with Git, managing dependencies (including co-development with the core github.com/etl-madness/flow library), and compiling all three ecosystem binaries across Windows, Linux, and macOS using every supported Go compiler option.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Architecture of the Build Ecosystem
  2. Prerequisites & Toolchain Verification
  3. Git Instructions (Clone, Tags, Branches & Co-Development)
  4. Quick Build: All Three Ecosystem Binaries
  5. Complete Reference of Supported go build Options
  6. Cross-Compilation Guide (Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM64)
  7. Air-Gapped & Offline Vendor Builds
  8. Automated Multi-Platform Release Scripts
  9. Running the Test Suite & Post-Build Verification
  10. Optional External Script Runtimes (dotnet-script & PowerShell pwsh)

docs.title: 1. Architecture of the Build Ecosystem
docs.text:
The go-flow repository contains three executable main packages and relies on 100% pure-Go database and cryptographic drivers, allowing you to compile zero-dependency static binaries without a C compiler (gcc/clang):

flowchart LR
    subgraph Repo["Git Repository: github.com/etl-madness/go-flow"]
        M1["Root Package (.)<br/>main.go, builder/, pkg/flowcrypto/"]
        M2["Crypto Utility (./crypto_tool)<br/>crypto_tool/main.go"]
        M3["SQL Importer (./db_importer)<br/>db_importer/mssql_importer.go"]
    end

    subgraph Deps["Pure-Go Embedded Drivers & Libraries"]
        D1["Core Engine: github.com/etl-madness/flow"]
        D2["Relational: go-mssqldb, lib/pq, mysql, go-ora/v2, modernc.org/sqlite"]
        D3["NoSQL & KV: bbolt, badger/v4, go-redis/v9, etcd/v3"]
        D4["Scripting & Crypto: Yaegi (Go), gopenpgp/v2, x/crypto"]
    end

    subgraph Binaries["Compiled Standalone Executables"]
        B1["flow / flow.exe<br/>(CLI Engine + HTMX Visual Studio)"]
        B2["crypto_tool / crypto_tool.exe<br/>(Keygen, Encrypt, Sign, Verify, Inspect)"]
        B3["db_importer / db_importer.exe<br/>(Database XML Repository Loader)"]
    end

    Deps --> Repo
    M1 --> B1
    M2 --> B2
    M3 --> B3
Target Binary Source Package Path Purpose flow / flow.exe . (Repository Root) Main ETL & workflow orchestration engine, schema validator, XSLT/Mermaid doc generator, and embedded HTMX Visual Pipeline Studio (-builder). crypto_tool / crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool Standalone CLI for RSA/Ed25519 key generation, AES-256-GCM encryption (FLOWENC:v1:), digital signing (FLOWSIGNED:v1:, .sig, .p7s), and verification. db_importer / db_importer.exe ./db_importer Bulk imports PipelineXML, OptionsXML, and ConfigXML files (UTF-8 or UTF-16) into SQL Server tables (dbo.flow_*_content).

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites & Toolchain Verification
docs.text:
1. Go SDK: Version 1.26.5 or newer (as specified in go.mod).
  2. Git: Version 2.30+ for cloning, tag checkout, and module resolution.
  3. C Compiler (Optional): Not required for standard or production builds (CGO_ENABLED=0 works natively). Only required if compiling with the -race data race detector enabled.

Verify your environment before building:

# Verify Go and Git versions
go version
git --version

# Inspect active Go environment variables (GOOS, GOARCH, CGO_ENABLED, GOMODCACHE)
go env GOOS GOARCH CGO_ENABLED GOPROXY

docs.title: 3.1 Clone the Repository (HTTPS or SSH)
docs.text:
# Option A: Clone via HTTPS
git clone https://github.com/etl-madness/go-flow.git
cd go-flow

# Option B: Clone via SSH
git clone git@github.com:etl-madness/go-flow.git
cd go-flow

docs.title: 3.2 Checkout a Specific Release Tag (Recommended for Production)
docs.text:
To build a deterministic release version (such as v1.1.24, v1.1.25, or v1.1.26):

# Fetch all remote tags
git fetch --all --tags

# List the 10 most recent semantic version tags
git tag --sort=-v:refname | head -n 10

# Checkout a specific release tag into a detached HEAD or release branch
git checkout tags/v1.1.26 -b release-v1.1.26

# Confirm exact commit hash and tag
git status
git rev-parse --short HEAD

docs.title: 3.3 Shallow Clone for Fast CI/CD Pipelines
docs.text:
In automated CI/CD runners (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps) where full commit history is unnecessary:

# Clone only the single commit for tag v1.1.26
git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.1.26 https://github.com/etl-madness/go-flow.git
cd go-flow

docs.title: 3.4 Updating an Existing Local Clone
docs.text:
# Pull latest changes on main and prune deleted remote branches
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git fetch --prune --prune-tags

# Synchronize and verify Go module dependencies against go.sum
go mod download
go mod verify

docs.title: 3.5 Co-Developing go-flow and flow Locally (Go Workspaces)
docs.text:
If you are modifying both github.com/etl-madness/go-flow (CLI & Visual Builder) and github.com/etl-madness/flow (Core Execution Engine) side-by-side:

# 1. Clone both repositories into the same parent directory (e.g., repos/etl-madness/)
cd ..
git clone https://github.com/etl-madness/flow.git
cd go-flow

# Option A: Use Go Workspace mode (Recommended — does not dirty go.mod)
go work init . ../flow
go work sync

# Option B: Temporary go.mod replace directive
go mod edit -replace github.com/etl-madness/flow=../flow
go mod tidy

# Revert the replace directive before committing to git:
go mod edit -dropreplace github.com/etl-madness/flow
go mod tidy

docs.title: 4. Quick Build: All Three Ecosystem Binaries
Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
# 1. Build the core Flow engine & HTMX Visual Builder
go build -o flow.exe .

# 2. Build the companion cryptographic utility
go build -o crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool

# 3. Build the SQL Server XML repository importer
go build -o db_importer.exe ./db_importer

docs.title: Linux & macOS (Bash / Zsh)
docs.text:
# 1. Build the core Flow engine & HTMX Visual Builder
go build -o flow .

# 2. Build the companion cryptographic utility
go build -o crypto_tool ./crypto_tool

# 3. Build the SQL Server XML repository importer
go build -o db_importer ./db_importer

docs.title: 5. Complete Reference of Supported go build Options
docs.text: Below is the comprehensive matrix of Go compiler, linker, and environment options supported when building flow, crypto_tool, and db_importer, along with copy-paste examples for each option.

docs.title: Summary Matrix of Build Options
docs.text: Option / Env Var Category Effect on go-flow Binaries Recommended For -o <path> Output Sets output executable path and filename (flow.exe, bin/flow). All builds CGO_ENABLED=0 Linker / Portability Disables cgo, producing a 100% static binary with zero libc/C dependencies. Production, Docker scratch / distroless / Alpine -trimpath Security / Reproducibility Strips all local filesystem paths (e.g., C:\Users\...) from the compiled binary and stack traces. Production & Security-Hardened Releases -ldflags="-s -w" Size Optimization Omits the symbol table (-s) and DWARF debug tables (-w), shrinking binary size by ~25–30%. Production & Edge Deployments -buildvcs=true\|false Provenance Embeds (or omits) Git commit SHA, timestamp, and dirty-tree status in Go build info (go version -m). CI/CD Auditing (true) or Reproducible (false) -mod=readonly Dependency Lock Fails the build if go.mod or go.sum needs updating, preventing accidental dependency drift. CI/CD Pipelines -mod=vendor Air-Gapped / Offline Compiles strictly using the local ./vendor directory without any network access. Air-Gapped / Restricted Enterprise Networks -race Concurrency Analysis Instruments memory access to detect data races in <parallel> workflows (requires CGO_ENABLED=1). QA, Integration Testing & Parallel Debugging -gcflags="all=-N -l" Interactive Debugging Disables compiler optimizations (-N) and function inlining (-l) for accurate breakpoints in Delve (dlv). Local Developer Debugging -pgo=auto Performance Applies Profile-Guided Optimization from default.pgo CPU profiles (~5–10% throughput boost). High-Volume Bulk ETL (<sql_bulk>, <kv_bulk>) -a Cache Control Forces recompilation of all packages, ignoring cached build artifacts in GOCACHE. Clean Release Builds -v / -x / -work Build Diagnostics Prints compiled package names (-v), exact compiler commands (-x), and preserves temp workdir (-work). Troubleshooting Toolchain Issues GOAMD64=v1..v4 CPU Microarchitecture Targets specific x86-64 instruction sets (v1 baseline SSE2, v3 AVX2/BMI2, v4 AVX-512). Hardware-Tuned Data Warehouse Servers

docs.title: Detailed Examples for Every Supported Option
5.1 Production Hardened & Size-Optimized Build (CGO_ENABLED=0, -trimpath, -ldflags="-s -w")
docs.text:
Produces a compact, reproducible, statically linked binary with no local filesystem paths leaked in panic traces:

# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:CGO_ENABLED = "0"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/flow.exe .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/db_importer.exe ./db_importer

# Linux / macOS (Bash)
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/flow .
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/db_importer ./db_importer

docs.title: 5.2 Embedding & Inspecting Git VCS Provenance (-buildvcs=true)
docs.text:
By default, Go embeds the exact Git commit hash, commit timestamp, and whether uncommitted modifications existed at build time. You can enforce this with -buildvcs=true and inspect any compiled flow binary using go version -m:

# Build with explicit VCS metadata stamping
go build -buildvcs=true -trimpath -o flow.exe .

# Inspect embedded Git commit, Go version, compiler flags, and module hashes
go version -m flow.exe

Sample go version -m output: 

flow.exe: go1.26.5
        path    github.com/etl-madness/go-flow
        mod     github.com/etl-madness/go-flow  (devel)
        dep     github.com/etl-madness/flow     v1.3.4
        build   -buildmode=exe
        build   -compiler=gc
        build   -trimpath=true
        build   vcs=git
        build   vcs.revision=a1b2c3d4e5f6...
        build   vcs.time=2026-10-31T12:00:00Z
        build   vcs.modified=false

docs.title: 5.3 Interactive Debugger Build (-gcflags="all=-N -l")
docs.text:
When stepping through flow or builder/ in VS Code, GoLand, or Delve (dlv), disable inlining and register optimizations so all local variables remain inspectable:

# Build with full DWARF symbols and optimizations disabled
go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o flow_debug.exe .

# Launch under Delve debugger
dlv exec ./flow_debug.exe -- -file pipeline.xml -debug

docs.title: 5.4 Data Race Detector Build (-race)
docs.text:
When testing complex <parallel> pipelines or custom Go extensions, compile with -race (requires CGO_ENABLED=1 and a C compiler such as MinGW-w64 gcc on Windows or build-essential on Linux):

# Windows (PowerShell with MinGW-w64 gcc in PATH)
$env:CGO_ENABLED = "1"
go build -race -o flow_race.exe .
./flow_race.exe -file parallel_pipeline.xml

# Linux / macOS
CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -race -o flow_race .
./flow_race -file parallel_pipeline.xml

docs.title: 5.5 CPU Microarchitecture Tuning (GOAMD64 & GOARM64)
docs.text:
For high-throughput <sql_bulk>, <kv_bulk>, and AES-256-GCM encryption on modern server hardware, target modern SIMD instruction sets:

# Target x86-64-v3 (AVX2, BMI2, FMA — Intel Haswell+ / AMD Excavator+ / modern cloud VMs)
GOAMD64=v3 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o flow_avx2.exe .

# Target x86-64-v4 (AVX-512 — Intel Skylake-X / Ice Lake+ / AMD Zen 4+)
GOAMD64=v4 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o flow_avx512.exe .

# Target ARM64 v9.0 with LSE atomics and crypto extensions (AWS Graviton3/4, Apple M-series)
GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 GOARM64=v9.0,lse,crypto CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o flow_graviton .

docs.title: 5.6 Diagnostic & Force-Rebuild Options (-a, -v, -x, -work)
docs.text:
When diagnosing build cache issues or auditing compiler invocations:

# Force full rebuild (-a) and print each package as it compiles (-v)
go build -a -v -o flow.exe .

# Print every underlying compiler/linker command (-x) and preserve temporary work directory (-work)
go build -x -work -o flow.exe .

docs.title: 6. Cross-Compilation Guide (Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM64)
docs.text: Because go-flow uses pure-Go drivers (modernc.org/sqlite, go-mssqldb, lib/pq, go-sql-driver/mysql, go-ora/v2, bbolt, badger), you can cross-compile for any operating system and CPU architecture from a single workstation by setting GOOS, GOARCH, and CGO_ENABLED=0.

docs.title: 6.1 Cross-Compiling from Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
# Ensure pure-Go static linking is enabled for all targets
$env:CGO_ENABLED = "0"

# 1. Windows x64 (amd64)
$env:GOOS = "windows"; $env:GOARCH = "amd64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-amd64/flow.exe .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-amd64/crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-amd64/db_importer.exe ./db_importer

# 2. Windows ARM64 (Surface / Windows on ARM)
$env:GOOS = "windows"; $env:GOARCH = "arm64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-arm64/flow.exe .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-arm64/crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-arm64/db_importer.exe ./db_importer

# 3. Linux x64 (amd64 — Ubuntu, RHEL, Debian, Alpine, Docker scratch)
$env:GOOS = "linux"; $env:GOARCH = "amd64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-amd64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-amd64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-amd64/db_importer ./db_importer

# 4. Linux ARM64 (AWS Graviton, Raspberry Pi 4/5, Kubernetes ARM nodes)
$env:GOOS = "linux"; $env:GOARCH = "arm64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-arm64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-arm64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-arm64/db_importer ./db_importer

# 5. macOS Apple Silicon (darwin/arm64 — M1/M2/M3/M4)
$env:GOOS = "darwin"; $env:GOARCH = "arm64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-arm64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-arm64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-arm64/db_importer ./db_importer

# 6. macOS Intel (darwin/amd64)
$env:GOOS = "darwin"; $env:GOARCH = "amd64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-amd64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-amd64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-amd64/db_importer ./db_importer

# 7. FreeBSD x64 & ARM64 (freebsd/amd64 & freebsd/arm64)
$env:GOOS = "freebsd"; $env:GOARCH = "amd64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-amd64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-amd64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-amd64/db_importer ./db_importer

$env:GOOS = "freebsd"; $env:GOARCH = "arm64"
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-arm64/flow .
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-arm64/crypto_tool ./crypto_tool

# Reset environment variables to host defaults

docs.title: 6.2 Cross-Compiling from Linux / macOS / FreeBSD (Bash / Sh)
docs.text:
# 1. Linux amd64 & arm64
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-amd64/flow .
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/linux-arm64/flow .

# 2. Windows amd64 & arm64
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-amd64/flow.exe .
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=windows GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/windows-arm64/flow.exe .

# 3. macOS Apple Silicon (arm64) & Intel (amd64)
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-arm64/flow .
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=darwin GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/darwin-amd64/flow .

# 4. FreeBSD amd64 & arm64
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=freebsd GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-amd64/flow .
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=freebsd GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/freebsd-arm64/flow .

Note on Platform-Specific PKCS#7 Signing (crypto_tool -format p7s): - Verification of .p7s (PKCS#7/CMS), .sig (OpenSSL), and .asc (OpenPGP) signatures is implemented in 100% pure Go (pkg/flowcrypto/pkcs7.go) and works identically across Windows, Linux, and macOS. - Signing in .p7s format using the Windows Certificate Store (-cert-thumbprint / -cert-store) invokes PowerShell's System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs.SignedCms when run on Windows, whereas -format sig (OpenSSL RSA/ECDSA/Ed25519) is pure Go on all platforms.

docs.title: 7. Air-Gapped & Offline Vendor Builds
docs.text:
For enterprise environments where build servers have no outbound internet access:

# Step 1 (On a connected machine): Vendor all module dependencies into ./vendor
git clone https://github.com/etl-madness/go-flow.git
cd go-flow
go mod tidy
go mod verify
go mod vendor

# Optional: Commit or archive the repository including ./vendor
tar -czf go-flow-vendored.tar.gz .

# Step 2 (On the air-gapped build server): Compile strictly from ./vendor
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOPROXY=off go build -mod=vendor -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o flow.exe .
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOPROXY=off go build -mod=vendor -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o crypto_tool.exe ./crypto_tool
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOPROXY=off go build -mod=vendor -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o db_importer.exe ./db_importer

docs.title: PowerShell Release Builder (build-all.ps1)
docs.text:
Builds all 3 binaries across all 6 target platforms and generates a SHA256SUMS.txt manifest:

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$targets = @(
    @{ GOOS = "windows"; GOARCH = "amd64"; Ext = ".exe" },
    @{ GOOS = "windows"; GOARCH = "arm64"; Ext = ".exe" },
    @{ GOOS = "linux";   GOARCH = "amd64"; Ext = ""     },
    @{ GOOS = "linux";   GOARCH = "arm64"; Ext = ""     },
    @{ GOOS = "darwin";  GOARCH = "amd64"; Ext = ""     },
    @{ GOOS = "darwin";  GOARCH = "arm64"; Ext = ""     },
    @{ GOOS = "freebsd"; GOARCH = "amd64"; Ext = ""     },
    @{ GOOS = "freebsd"; GOARCH = "arm64"; Ext = ""     }
)

$env:CGO_ENABLED = "0"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "dist" | Out-Null
$hashes = @()

foreach ($t in $targets) {
    $env:GOOS = $t.GOOS
    $env:GOARCH = $t.GOARCH
    $outDir = "dist/$($t.GOOS)-$($t.GOARCH)"
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $outDir | Out-Null

    Write-Host "Building $($t.GOOS)/$($t.GOARCH)..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
    go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o "$outDir/flow$($t.Ext)" .
    go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o "$outDir/crypto_tool$($t.Ext)" ./crypto_tool
    go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o "$outDir/db_importer$($t.Ext)" ./db_importer

    Get-ChildItem -Path $outDir -File | ForEach-Object {
        $h = (Get-FileHash $_.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower()
        $rel = "$($t.GOOS)-$($t.GOARCH)/$($_.Name)"
        $hashes += "$h  $rel"
    }
}

$hashes | Set-Content -Path "dist/SHA256SUMS.txt" -Encoding UTF8
Remove-Item Env:GOOS, Env:GOARCH, Env:CGO_ENABLED -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Write-Host "Release build complete! Checksums written to dist/SHA256SUMS.txt" -ForegroundColor Green

docs.title: 9. Running the Test Suite & Post-Build Verification
docs.text:
After cloning or modifying the repository, run the automated test suite and smoke-test the compiled binaries:

# 1. Run all unit & integration tests across the entire repository
go test ./...

# 2. Run specific package tests with verbose output
go test -v .
go test -v ./builder
go test -v ./pkg/flowcrypto
go test -v ./crypto_tool
go test -v ./db_importer

# 3. Verify the compiled binaries respond to CLI flags
./flow -h
./crypto_tool -h
./db_importer -h

# 4. Validate a sample pipeline against the XSD schema without executing
./flow -file scripts.xml -xsd ./xsd/pipeline.xsd -validate

docs.title: 10. Optional External Script Runtimes (dotnet-script & PowerShell pwsh)
docs.text:
By default, <script language="go"> runs in-process via the embedded pure-Go Yaegi interpreter and requires zero external tools. However, if your pipelines use C# scripts (<script language="csx">) or cross-platform PowerShell 7+ (<script language="pwsh">), you can install those optional runtimes from the command line as shown below.

<script> Language Attribute Runtime Binary Invoked Bundled in flow? When Installation Is Needed language="go" Embedded Yaegi engine Yes (Built-in) Never — compiled directly into flow. language="sh" / "bash" / "zsh" / "cmd" Host OS shell OS Built-in Included on standard POSIX / Windows hosts. language="csx" dotnet-script Optional external Required only if pipelines execute C# .csx <script> nodes. language="pwsh" pwsh (PowerShell 7+) Optional external Required on Linux, macOS, FreeBSD (or Windows for PS7+) when using language="pwsh".

docs.title: 10.1 Installing dotnet-script via Command Line (for <script language="csx">)
docs.text: dotnet-script is distributed as a cross-platform .NET Global Tool and works on Windows, Linux, macOS, and FreeBSD wherever the .NET SDK (dotnet 8.0+) is installed.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the .NET SDK (if not already installed)
docs.text:
# Windows (via winget)
winget install Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.8

# Ubuntu / Debian Linux
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y dotnet-sdk-8.0

# RHEL / Rocky / AlmaLinux / Fedora
sudo dnf install -y dotnet-sdk-8.0

# macOS (via Homebrew)
brew install --cask dotnet-sdk

# FreeBSD (via pkg)
sudo pkg install -y dotnet

docs.title: Step 2: Install dotnet-script Globally via dotnet tool
docs.text:
# Install the latest stable dotnet-script global tool
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-script

# (Optional) Update an existing installation to the latest version
dotnet tool update -g dotnet-script

# (Optional) Install a specific pinned version for reproducible CI environments
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-script --version 1.6.0

docs.title: Step 3: Ensure ~/.dotnet/tools Is in PATH and Verify
docs.text:
# Windows (PowerShell) — automatically added by the SDK installer, or add for current session:
$env:PATH += ";$HOME\.dotnet\tools"
dotnet-script --version
dotnet-script eval "Console.WriteLine(21 * 2);"

# Linux / macOS / FreeBSD (Bash / Zsh / Sh)
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.dotnet/tools"
# Persist in ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.profile:
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.dotnet/tools"' >> ~/.profile

# Verify dotnet-script execution
dotnet-script --version
dotnet-script eval 'Console.WriteLine("dotnet-script ready on " + Environment.OSVersion);'

docs.title: 10.2 Installing PowerShell (pwsh) on Linux, macOS & FreeBSD (for <script language="pwsh">)
docs.text: When a pipeline step uses <script language="pwsh">, Flow invokes the cross-platform pwsh executable.

docs.title: A. Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, Alpine)
docs.text:
# Ubuntu / Debian (via Microsoft Package Repository)
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y wget apt-transport-https software-properties-common
source /etc/os-release
wget -q "https://packages.microsoft.com/config/${ID}/${VERSION_ID}/packages-microsoft-prod.deb"
sudo dpkg -i packages-microsoft-prod.deb && rm packages-microsoft-prod.deb
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y powershell

# RHEL 8/9, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Fedora (via dnf)
sudo dnf install -y https://packages.microsoft.com/config/rhel/9/packages-microsoft-prod.rpm
sudo dnf install -y powershell

# Universal Linux Alternative (via Snap)
sudo snap install powershell --classic

docs.title: B. macOS (Intel & Apple Silicon)
docs.text:
# Install PowerShell 7+ via Homebrew Cask
brew install --cask powershell

# Verify installation
pwsh -Version

docs.title: C. FreeBSD (and Any OS with the .NET SDK Installed)
docs.text:
On FreeBSD (as well as minimal Linux containers or non-root environments), PowerShell can be installed directly as a .NET Global Tool using the dotnet CLI:

# 1. Install the .NET SDK on FreeBSD (if not already present)
sudo pkg install -y dotnet

# 2. Install PowerShell (pwsh) as a .NET Global Tool
dotnet tool install --global PowerShell

# 3. Ensure ~/.dotnet/tools is on PATH
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.dotnet/tools"

# 4. Verify pwsh in non-interactive mode
pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command '$PSVersionTable.PSVersion'
